Ata da Sessão Solene de Defesa da Dissertação do Curso de Mestrado em Ciência da Computação-UFS. Candidato: ARTUR LEANDRO DA COSTA OLIVEIRA

Em 08 dias do mês de junho do ano de dois mil e vinte dois, com início às 14h00min, realizou-se na Sala de Reunião do PROCC da Universidade Federal de Sergipe, na Cidade Universitária Prof. José Aloísio de Campos, a Sessão Pública de Defesa de Dissertação de Mestrado do candidato Artur Leandro da Costa Oliveira , que desenvolveu o trabalho intitulado: ' A Framework for Inverse Modeling Applied to Multi-objective Evolutionary Algorithms ', sob a orientação do Prof. Dr. André Britto de Carvalho . A Sessão foi presidida pelo Prof. Dr. André Britto de Carvalho (PROCC/UFS), que após a apresentação da dissertação passou a palavra aos outros membros da Banca Examinadora, Prof. Dr. Renato Tinos (USP) e, em seguida, o Prof. Dr. Leonardo Nogueira Matos (PROCC/UFS) e o Prof. Dr. Renê Pereira de Gusmão (PROCC/UFS). ## Abstract

Many-Objective Optimization Problems (MaOPs) are a class of complex optimization problems defined by having more than three objective functions. Traditional Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms (MOEAs) have shown poor scalability in solving this kind of problem. The use of machine learning techniques to enhance optimization algorithms applied to MaOPs has been drawing attention due to their capacity to add domain knowledge during the search process. One method of this kind is inverse modeling, which uses machine learning models to enhance MOEAs differently, mapping the objective function values to the decision variables. This method has shown a good performance in diverse optimization problems due to the ability to directly predict solutions closed to the Pareto-optimal front, among these methods, we can highlight the Decision Variable Learning (DVL). The strategies involving inverse models found, including the DVL, have some limitations such as the exploration of the performance of different machine learning models and the strategies in using the generated knowledge during the search. The main goal of this work is to create a framework that uses an inverse modeling approach coupled to any MOEA found in the literature. More precisely, three main steps were taken to achieve the goals. First, we perform a systematic review of the literature to identify the main uses of machine learning techniques enhancing optimization algorithms. Secondly, we analyze the performance of different machine learning methods in the DVL, seeking to understand the main characteristics of inverse modeling through the DVL algorithm. In the last step, we propose a framework that is an extension of the DVL algorithm, based on the knowledge obtained in the systematic review and our analysis of the DVL. This framework results in an algorithm for MaOPs recommended for situations that exist restrictions on the number of evaluations in the objective function.

Keywords ȷ multi-objective optimization, machine learning, inverse models.

## 1

## Introduction

Multi-Objective Problems (MOPs) are a class of optimization problems that involves more than one conflicting objective function to be optimized simultaneously (COELLO et al., 2007). Due to the conflict between the objective functions, there is not a single solution able to optimize all the objectives, but a resulting set is achieved with the best solutions. To obtain this solution set, we use the Pareto Optimality Theory (COELLO et al., 2007). Metaheuristics is the name given to the most general kind of optimization algorithms (LUKE, 201«) that are applied to a very wide range of problems. Usually, MOPs can be solved by Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms (MOEAs), such as Genetic Algorithms (GAs), Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), among others. MOEAs are based on Evolutionary algorithms (EAs), which is a class of population-based search metaheuristic.

MOEAs have been shown to perform well on a wide range of MOPs with two or three objective functions. However, with the growth of this area, several problems with a high degree of complexity have been found making most of MOEAs facing difficulties to solve them. Most of these complex problems are real-world problems and difficulties faced by the algorithms are often because some of these problems are discontinuous, non-differential, with many good locations, or because of the difficulty these problems present in evaluating a solution such as ambiguity, noise, and slowness to evaluate (SHI; RASHEED, 2010). Another well-known class of complex problems that MOEAs have experienced substantial difficulties to solve is the Many-Objective Optimization Problems (MaOPs), which have more than three objective functions (SCHUTZE; LARA; COELLO, 2010). The MaOPs have attracted increasing attention in the evolutionary optimization field (LI et al., 2015).

The poor scalability of traditional MOEAs in solving MaOPs has triggered a sizeable amount of research, aiming to provide alternative approaches that can properly handle this kind of problem (MARTÍ et al., 2010). A set of these approaches proposes to obtain knowledge of the domain during the search process or by external knowledge that could lead to enhance the search.

They are most motivated by the amount of available data created during the search, which leads to better handle the MaOPs. The objective of this approach is to extract information hidden in the data, which contains the behavior of the distribution of population individuals in the searching space, the landscape with a feasible area of convergence, and the relationship between the Pareto front and the Pareto optimally set (FAN et al., 2016). A way to extract this knowledge is by incorporating machine learning algorithms and techniques in the MOEAs.

The combination of optimization algorithms with machine learning techniques has been the subject of research in the last few years. The existing literature in this area can be divided into two main groupsȷ the first one is concerned in improving the performance of machine learning techniques with metaheuristics, and the second group relies on the use of machine learning for enhancing metaheuristics (CALVET et al., 2017). Regarding the first group, different metaheuristic algorithms successfully improve the performance of machine learning techniques. This enhancement acts in optimizing machine learning models areas, such as parameters and architecture. The second group, which is the theme of this systematic review, can be viewed as knowledge extraction and integration into the optimization process. This knowledge can take different forms and result in different ways of integrating the knowledge into the metaheuristic (TALBI, 2016). Three different criteria are used to refine the classification of this kind of integrationȷ Time of Hybridization, Aim of Hybridization, and Involved Component. Time of Hybridization relies on the time of extracting knowledge from the optimization process. The Aim of the Hybridization is about the result of the integration. The Involved Component classifies in which area of the algorithm the integration occurs.

Some known algorithms approaches that employs machine learning models to enhance metaheuristics are the Estimation of Distribution Algorithms (EDAs) (LARRAÑAGA; LOZANO, 2001) and Surrogate-Assisted Evolutionary Algorithms (SAEAs) (JIN, 2011). EDAs are variants of the evolutionary algorithms that at each iteration extract knowledge from the solutions found and build a probabilistic model, which replaces the common GAs operators of crossover and mutation. The motivation of this method is to understand the relationship between the variables and use it to explore the search domain. The SAEAs uses surrogates, also know as metamodels, to substitute the real objective function. Mainly motivated from reducing computational time in evolutionary optimization of expensive problems, such as aerodynamic design optimization or drug design, where complex simulations are involved. The idea behind SAEAs is that, if a surrogate model of the real expensive function can be created with relatively few samples, and also few evaluations, then this surrogate model can be used instead of the expensive objective function in the optimization process. Different strategies are driven from these ideas that lead to make SAEAs a good approach to solve real-world applications (JIN, 2011).

Motivated by the metamodel used in SAEAs algorithms, an inverse model of the problem is proposed in (GIAGKIOZIS; FLEMING, 2012; GIAGKIOZIS; FLEMING, 201»). Differently from the surrogate in the SAEAs, the inverse model maps the objective function values to the

decision variables, being capable of understanding the Pareto-optimal set and propose an optimal solution set. In their work, this inverse model is used to generate more non-dominated solutions for the decision-maker (DM), based on the approximated Pareto set obtained by MOEAs at the end of evolutionary optimization, increasing the density of the Pareto set found. Their method is further improved in many aspects, Kudikala, Giagkiozis &amp; Fleming (201«b), Kudikala, Giagkiozis &amp; Fleming (201«a) proposes the use of clustering methods to separate the search space for training the inverse model increasing the number of non-dominated solutions generated. The work in (YAN; GIAGKIOZIS; FLEMING, 2015) studies how the samples of the inverse model can improve the final solutions predictions and propose an evolutionary algorithm that provides betters samples for training the inverse model. The inverse model can be also used as the probabilistic model in an EDA variant algorithm like the one proposed in (CHENG et al., 2015).

Recently, Santos, Oliveira &amp; Britto (2019) proposed an algorithm denominated Decision Variable Learning (DVL), which uses the concept of the inverse model differently. Instead of using the model to generate more non-dominated solutions or to modeling the operators of an evolutionary algorithm as the EDAs, the inverse model in this work is used to directly predict the Pareto-optimal set. Their method runs standalone, without the presence of an optimization algorithm like the methods previously explained. In their experiments, the DVL surpassed the NSGA-III (DEB; JAIN, 201»), a classic algorithm from literature, in some benchmarks problems, in situations where there is a restriction in the number of evaluations of the objective function and when there is a high number of objectives.

The strategies involving inverse models found have some limitations, one of them is the exploration of the performance of different machine learning models. In the works found, only a few different models were used, and no experimental comparison was made with well-known machine learning models in the literature to realize this kind of task. Another limitation is related to the strategy in using the generated knowledge during the search. In each work, the inverse modeling is applied in different ways, and despite the good results, there is no clarity on the best way to use the knowledge, as well as an understanding of the expected effects. For example, inverse modeling for generating more non-dominated solutions in (GIAGKIOZIS; FLEMING, 201») has encountered a positive side effect. On many test instances, the estimated Pareto set turns out to be superior to the initial set. This assumption, coupled with the work developed in the DVL algorithm, shows that exists a research area to be developed on the estimation of the Pareto-optimal set. Further experimentation can be carried out to validate the hypothesis that it is possible to estimate the Pareto set with the decision variables. A well-defined set of benchmark test instances, and the use of different machine learning models and techniques could be used to validate the method. Also, the combination of the DVL with an MOEA could lead to mutual improvement between algorithms. While the DVL estimates the Pareto set with a low number of evaluations, the MOEA could lead the population predicted by the DVL to better convergence and divergence of the Pareto front. For this, some improvements in the design of the DVL algorithm have to be done to achieve this combination. Also, the specification of a

framework, for this reason, can abstract the method to be used with any MOEA benefiting from the use of different MOEAs for MOPs and MaOPs.

## 1.1 Objectives of the research

The main objective of this work is to create a framework that uses an inverse modeling approach coupled to any MOEA found in the literature. More precisely, three main steps were taken to achieve the goals. First, we perform a systematic review of the literature to identify the main uses of machine learning techniques enhancing optimization algorithms. Secondly, we analyze the performance of different machine learning methods in the DVL, seeking to understand the main characteristics of inverse modeling through the DVL algorithm. In the last step, we propose a framework that is an extension of the DVL algorithm, based on the knowledge obtained in the systematic review and our analysis of the DVL. This framework results in an algorithm for MaOPs recommended for situations that exist restrictions on the number of evaluations in the objective function. It uses a modified generic version of the DVL algorithm, which contains an inverse model of the problem inside to interact with the MOEA during the search. This DVL version needs to be adaptable in terms of machine learning models for a better understanding of different optimization problems, and the algorithm must have a computational complexity as close as possible to the MOEA coupled to it, to not slow the search process.

## 1.1.1 Specific objectives

The following specific objectives were defined to achieve the main objectiveȷ

1. Perform a systematic review of the literature of machine learning methods enhancing metaheuristics;
2. Validate the hypothesis that inverse models can be used to estimate the Pareto optimal set;
3. «. Propose a DVL variation that can be used in union with other MOEAs inside a framework;
4. ». Propose a framework that uses the DVL variation for generating new (and promising) solutions in multi-objective optimization.
5. Validate the framework in different scenarios of multi-objective optimization.

## 1.1.2 Methodology

This research work is characterized as applied research that contains exploratory and descriptive objectives, with a qualitative approach of bibliographic character and experimental, composed of five parts. The first part consists of a systematic review of the literature of machine learning methods enhancing metaheuristics. At this point, the general state of the art of the

problem will be analyzed and acquired the theoretical background necessary to develop this work. In the second part, we study the literature in depth to find possible approaches that use inverse models with metaheuristics. This part assists us in proposing this research and provides knowledge of the studied field used by some researchers.

The third part consists of deep experimentation over inverse models. Where diverse machine learning techniques are explored to validate their performance in estimating the Pareto optimal set. In the fourth step, we propose an algorithm that is a variation of the DVL, and a framework for the use of different strategies of the DVL inverse modeling in multi-objective optimization. This algorithm uses the inverse model to predict new solutions nearest to the Pareto optimal set and send these solutions to the MOEA to improve the search process. The framework correspond to the different ways of integration between the algorithms. The validation of our proposed framework is executed in the fifth step, where experiments with different MOEAs are made in several multi-objective optimization problems. The new proposed framework need to improve the performance of the MOEAs according to some metrics of the literature in optimization problems.

## 1.2 Document Structure

This document is organized into chapters and sections to facilitate understanding, provide better navigation and allow a better reading of the document. The main steps of this work were organized into three main chaptersȷ chapter 2 - Theoretical Background with the Systematic Review, chapter « - DVL validation, and chapter » - DVL framework. Chapters « and » were organized separately, each one containing an explanation of the methods, the experiments, and the results obtained. Each chapter of the document is well described belowȷ

1. Chapter 1 - Introductionȷ presents the preliminary definitions of the literature, problematic, arguments and hypothesis on the topic, in addition to the objectives, and the proposed methodology to achieve these objectives;
2. Chapter 2 - Theoretical Backgroundȷ describes the theoretical context, with the revision of literature (Systematic Review) related to the proposed theme, as well as the results of this review and synthesis of the summary process of the studies, and finally a discussion about inverse models;
3. «. Chapter « - Validating DVL Performanceȷ define the steps made to prove the hypotheses that inverse models can be used to estimate the Pareto optimal set;
4. ». Chapter » - DVL Frameworkȷ define the architecture of the framework and the reasons for such design, and validate the framework with different MOEAs in a set of multi-objective optimization problems.

5. Chapter 5 - Conclusionȷ resumes the hypothesis validations found and the results of the experiments. And also exposes the open research areas and future directions over the DVL.

## Theoretical Background

## 2.1 Overview

## 2.1.1 Stochastic Optimization

The field of Stochastic Optimization represents optimization methodologies that employ some degree of randomness to find optimal solutions as possible to hard optimization problems. Usually, these kinds of problems cannot be solved optimally, or to any guaranteed bound, by any exact (deterministic) method within a 'reasonable' time limit (BOUSSAÏD; LEPAGNOT; SIARRY, 201«). An important subset of optimization problems is the ones that present more than one objective function. They are normally called multi-objective optimization problems (MOPs). In general, MOPs can be defined as followsȷ

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

where X = ( /u1D465 1 , /u1D465 2 , ..., /u1D465 /u1D45B ) /u1D447 ∈ Ω constitutes the decision variable (vector), Ω is the decision space, /u1D445 /u1D45A is the objective space, and /u1D439 : Ω → /u1D445 /u1D45A is a mapping from the decision space to the objective space composing of /u1D45A real-value evaluation functions (FAN et al., 2016). Generally, in the MOPs, no single point in the decision space can reach the optimum in each objective simultaneously. So the solutions set are found through the use of the Pareto Optimality Theory (COELLO et al., 2007). Where, considering a minimization problem, a decision vector X /u1D462 ∈ Ω is said to dominate other vector X /u1D463 ∈ Ω (denoted by X /u1D462 ≺ X /u1D463 ) if and only if /u1D439 ( X /u1D462 ) is partially less than /u1D439 ( X /u1D463 ) , i.e. /u1D453 /u1D456 ( X /u1D462 ) ≤ /u1D453 /u1D456 ( X /u1D463 ) , ∀ /u1D456 ∈ { 1 , ..., /u1D45A } and /u1D439 ( X /u1D462 ) ≠ /u1D439 ( X /u1D463 ) . The set of vectors that cannot be dominated by any other point from the decision space is defined as Pareto-optimal set (PS), the map of the PS to the objective space is defined as the Pareto Front (PF). Other well-known classes of complex problems are the Many-Objective Optimization

Problems (MaOPs), which have more than three objective functions. This kind of problem has attracted increased attention in evolutionary optimization by the difficulties faced in solving them (FLEMING; PURSHOUSE; LYGOE, 2005).

Metaheuristics are the most general kind of optimization algorithms (LUKE, 201«), they are applied to find satisfactory solutions for optimization problems. They can be classified as single-solution based metaheuristics, whereas are more exploitation-oriented, such as Simulated Annealing, Tabu Search, GRASP, Guided Local Search, Iterated Local Search, etc. And can be classified as Population-Based Metaheuristics that are more exploration-orientedȷ Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) and Swarm Intelligence (BOUSSAÏD; LEPAGNOT; SIARRY, 201«). The use of Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms (MOEAs) to solve optimization problems has been motivated mainly because of the population-based nature of EAs. Also, these algorithms use mechanisms based on Pareto optimality that avoids convergence to a single solution preserving the diversity of the PF. Some real-world optimization problems drive the use of non-traditional approaches, mainly due to large search spaces, uncertainty, noise, disjoint Pareto curves, etc (COELLO et al., 2007). It is known that MOEAs scale poorly, facing serious difficulties in solving MaOPs. Primary because of the exponential increase in the number of non-dominated solutions in each population, putting pressure towards the Pareto-optimal front. Consequently, the convergence property of MOEAs is deteriorated (SCHUTZE; LARA; COELLO, 2010).

## 2.1.2 Machine Learning

Machine Learning (ML) is a subfield of computer science and artificial intelligence that studies and design algorithms which learn from data, composed by observations, and make predictions based on these data (PROVOST; KOHAVI, 1998). ML simulates human learning by acquiring knowledge from the real world. Formally, (ANDERSON, 1990) defines ML as followsȷ 'A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E'.

A large set of ML algorithms is proposed in the literature. They can be classified by the human supervision on training (DEY, 2016). There is four main types of this classificationȷ Supervised Learning, Unsupervised Learning, Semisupervised Learning, and Reinforcement Learning. In Supervised Learning, the algorithm is provided with training data and correct answers. Its task is to learn with the training data and predict outputs, based on provided data, as close as possible to the expected answers. Typical tasks of Supervised Learning are classification and regression.

In Unsupervised Learning, the algorithm does not have correct answers for the training data. In this type of ML system, instead of predict expected values, the algorithm tries to capture some characteristics of the training data and the observed random variables. Typical tasks of the Unsupervised Learning are clustering, visualization and dimensionality reduction, and

association rule learning. Semisupervised Learning is when the algorithm is provided with a training set with missing information, some answers are labeled some do not have any information. Most Semisupervised learning algorithms are combinations of Unsupervised and Supervised algorithms.

Reinforcement Learning uses a learning system as an agent that interacts with the environment. Based on these interactions, the learning system can select and perform actions and get rewards or be punished for its choices. The goal in the Reinforcement Learning system is to train the agent to maximize the expected sum of future rewards, called the return. As an example, many robots use this kind of learning system to learn how to move.

Diverse algorithms and techniques detailed in the literature are capable of performing machine learning tasks (DEY, 2016). For Supervised Learning, a well-known algorithm is the Decision Tree, which uses trees as data structure, it starts with a root node and ends with a decision made by the leaves that generate the predicted result. The decision nodes group attributes by sorting them based on their values. Naïve Bayes, is a method that depends on the conditional probability to classify or cluster the dataset. Support Vector Machine (SVM), widely used in machine learning, works on the principle of margin calculation, it draws margins between the classes and uses these margins for minimizing the classification error. For Unsupervised Learning, the k-means algorithm is a widely used clustering method for this task that creates /u1D458 distinct clusters around centroids calculated by the features. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is another unsupervised method that has as principal function the reduction of the dimension of the data to make the computation faster and easier.

For Semisupervised Learning, the Generative models are one of the oldest semisupervised methods that use a mixed distribution e.g. Gaussian mixture models to identify the unlabeled data. Self-training is a technique that uses a classifier trained with a portion of labeled data, and afterward, this classifier is fed with unlabeled data to predict their labels. And the Transductive SVM, which is an extension of the SVM method to work in Semisupervised Learning (DEY, 2016). For Reinforcement learning, the Markov Decision Process (MDP) maps the process of the agent interacting with the environment. And Q-learning (WATKINS; DAYAN, 1992), a model-free algorithm that learns the value of an action in a particular state.

Another important method, widely used in the literature is the artificial neural network (ANN) (WANG, 200«). Inspired by the sophisticated functionality of human brains, it can be used in diverse machine learning tasks. ANN consists of an input layer, one or more hidden layers of neurons, and a final layer of output neurons. That construction can approximate any computable function to arbitrary precision. The numbers given to the input are independent variables, and the numbers to the output are dependent variables that map the function in question. The input and outputs of an ANN can be transformed to take different forms, such as number, binary, and label. Allowing the ability to be applied in a wide range of tasks.

## 2.1.3 Machine Learning Enhancing Metaheuristics

An overview of the interaction between Optimization and Machine learning can be found in (CALVET et al., 2017), which analyses and discusses the different areas where these two fields of computer science can combine. Figure 1 shows this interaction and also describes some relevant and representative topics. The intersection of the two areas can be divided into Enhancing Metaheuristics and Improve ML techniques. The first one is the theme of our systematic review, well detailed in section 2.2, while the second one references the improvement that metaheuristics can make to ML techniques.

Figure 1 - Classification of works combining metaheuristics and machine learning.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Sourceȷ (CALVET et al., 2017)

The subarea of machine learning enhancing metaheuristics algorithms is well detailed in (JOURDAN; DHAENENS; TALBI, 2006; TALBI, 2016), where classifications of the area are well proposed by these papers. Besides the differences in terminologies of these works, the concepts remain the same. Figure 2 shows the three main types of this enhancement. Time of hybridization concerns to when the knowledge is extracted. Off-line strategies extract the knowledge before the search starts, while online strategies extract the knowledge dynamically during the search. The Aim of hybridization concerns to the impact of the result between the integration of the two areas. Integration based on Efficiency improves the search time by reducing the search space or by approximating the objective function. Effectiveness incorporates knowledge to the search, leading to a better quality of solutions. The last type is the Involved component, usually, metaheuristics can be divided into different search components. This classification corresponds to the place in the metaheuristic where the machine learning component was inserted.

Figure 2 - Classification of enhancing metaheuristics with machine learning.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Sourceȷ (TALBI, 2016)

In our systematic review, the terms presented in Figure 2 will be used for the classification of the papers, except for the Involved component. About this criteria, we prefer to use the terms of the taxonomy proposed by (ZHANG et al., 2011), shown in Figure «. Their taxonomy details all components involved in integration with machine learning on Evolutionary Computation (EC), which can be abstract to any kind of metaheuristic algorithm. The Evolutionary algorithm can be divided into 5 main areasȷ Population Initialization, Fitness Evaluation and Selection, Population Reproduction and Variation, Algorithm Adaptation, and Local Search (LS). Population Initialization is the first step on an Evolutionary algorithm, generally, metaheuristics produce the initial population randomly. The integration with ML can benefit this step by organizing the initial population and changing the decision vector to improve solutions quality. Other techniques use historical search experience to generate this initial set.

The Machine Learning method used in the Fitness Evaluation and Selection step aims to model the objective function or reduce the number of evaluations. Population Reproduction and Variation is a crucial step with much attention in the optimization literature. In this step, ML techniques can generate new solutions with embedded knowledge about the problem. This knowledge can reduce the problem scale, help in diversity and convergence of new solutions, and predict promising regions. Algorithm Adaptation refers to the algorithm as a whole, where ML is used to improve the optimization parameters and operators. The last taxonomy refers to the Local Search (LS), where the ML can be used to design, choose when to use, and control the different local search strategies.

In addition to the studies presented above, other papers found in the literature aggregated value to prepare our systematic review. The papers in (PELIKAN; GOLDBERG; LOBO, 2002; BENGIO; LODI; PROUVOST, 2020; FAN et al., 2016) contribute by identifying search terms for our research method and describe base algorithms that are used by other algorithms that enhance metaheuristics. Also, they show different application areas that this kind of algorithm can be used.

## 2.1.4 Inverse Modeling

Methods based on surrogates have gained prominence in recent years. In the context of MOPs, most of the related work focuses on constructing learning models to predict several objective functions, from the decision variable as an input. They provide approximate models to represent the original problem in a way that facilitates solving it by optimization algorithms, surrogates can also be called metamodels. There are several metamodeling methods, but they can be divided into two main categories (SHI; RASHEED, 2010)ȷ classic function transformation methods and surrogate modeling methods. The first category corresponds to the techniques that seek to represent the set of functions of the problem to a simpler one, such as transforming it into a linear function or using classical methods to approximate the problem functions by finding a weighted sum of simpler functions. The second category seeks a new expression for each objective function that is constructed based on the data obtained previously from the real objective function, called surrogates (SANTANA-QUINTERO; MONTANO; COELLO, 2010). There are three main ways to create surrogates, from instance-based learning models, machine learning, and statistical learning.

In (SHI; RASHEED, 2010), a study on methods of approaching function in optimization problems is made. In this work, a division is presented between the methods of approximation, which are the classical methods of function transformation and surrogate modeling methods. Also, the paper describes the types of surrogate-based methods that were separated into learning models based on instances, machine learning, and statistical learning. In (SANTANA-QUINTERO; MONTANO; COELLO, 2010), the authors seek to analyze several techniques to deal with functions with high computational costs. For this, they approach the concept of incorporation of information in optimization problems. According to the authors, there are three main ways to do thisȷ problem approximation, which tries to replace the problem with one that is very close to it, but which is easier to solve; functional approximation (Metamodels); and evolutionary approximation, which is specific to evolutionary algorithms, this approach attempts to reduce function evaluations by estimating the adequacy of an individual from other similar individuals. This work also analyzes some real problems that were solved using some techniques studied in the paper.

However, despite the existence of related work on surrogates applied to multi- and many-objective optimization, they only explore learning from decision variables to model the objective functions. During our study of surrogates some questions aroseȷ

1. Since in MaOPs we have objective vectors with higher dimensions, could it be possible to learn the behavior from objective functions to estimate the decision variables?
2. Since it is possible to learn the behavior from decision variables using surrogates, is it possible to learn inverse functions and from that functions, to predict sub-optimal solutions to the problem?

According to our research, the first attempt of constructing an inverse modeling method is made in Giagkiozis &amp; Fleming (2012), Giagkiozis &amp; Fleming (201»), called Pareto Estimation (PE). Where an inverse functional mapping from PF to PS was built based on the non-dominated solutions set obtained by the execution of an MOEA at the end of evolutionary optimization. This model is used to generate additional non-dominated solutions, thereby enhancing the density of the solutions set. Their motivation is that in many MOPs, principally in MaOPs, the decision-maker (DM) is not satisfied with the Pareto set (PS) obtained by the MAOE. This method alleviates these difficulties for continuous optimization problems by producing more and, usually, better distributed Pareto optimal solutions along the entire Pareto front (PF). In these works, it should be noted that the inverse model is not used during the optimization process.

The general approach, when substituting the real objective function with a surrogate model for use in an EA, has the following stepsȷ

1. Sample the real objective function.

2. Use the obtained samples to create a surrogate model.
2. «. Use the surrogate model in the optimization.
3. ». If the convergence criteria are met, stop; if not, go to Step 1.

An illustration of the metamodeling process in comparison with the PE method can be seen in Figure ». Where /u1D446 ∈ R /u1D45B is the decision space, /u1D44D ∈ R /u1D45A is the objective space, and /u1D439 : /u1D446 → /u1D44D the objective function of the optimization problem. The function ˆ /u1D439 represents the surrogate or metamodel created a priori or in every iteration ( ˆ /u1D439 0 , ˆ /u1D439 1 , ..., ˆ /u1D439 /u1D45B ) of the optimization process. Different metamodel approaches are well detailed in (DEB et al., 2019), where a taxonomy of frameworks is proposed to help solve multi-objective optimization problems. They also present a comparative study of the results obtained by the frameworks.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Also, in Figure » the set /u1D437 represents the non-dominated set and /u1D443 the Pareto Front (PF) of the objectives from /u1D437 . In the Pareto Estimation method is possible to verify that the inverse

model ˜ /u1D439 /u1D443 : ˜ /u1D443 → /u1D437 uses a set ˜ /u1D443 as input for training. This set ˜ /u1D443 is the result of the normalization of the set /u1D443 scaled to the range [ 0 , 1 ] . To perform the approximation of the inverse function the researchers use a Radial Basis Function Neural Network (RBFNN). In their experiments, the use of the PE method increases the number of non-dominated solutions along the surface, enhancing the ability of the DM to identify the best solutions. Also, a positive side effect is encountered in their experiments that were not in the intended purpose of the method, in some test instances, the generated solutions by the inverse model have superior values in comparison to the set provided by the MOEA.

Enhancements of the PE method can be obtained in the literature. In (KUDIKALA; GIAGKIOZIS; FLEMING, 201«b; KUDIKALA; GIAGKIOZIS; FLEMING, 201«a) the PE method is extended to improve the density of available non-dominated solutions in multi-objective multi-modal problems. This kind of problem has multiples decision vectors that map to identical objective vectors on the Pareto front. In this case, the authors propose to subdivide the objective space, by using a clustering algorithm, into different /u1D436 /u1D45A clusterings. So an ANN is trained for each cluster of solutions to identify the map ˜ /u1D439 ˜ /u1D443 /u1D436 /u1D45A : ˜ /u1D443 → /u1D436 /u1D45A . In these works, it is noted that the quality of the resulting inverse model depends heavily on the training samples used. So in (YAN; GIAGKIOZIS; FLEMING, 2015) is proposed the MAEA-GD/RD an optimization algorithm based on the MAEA-gD with sample redistribution, which reallocates the samples in the current population in objective space for training the inverse model. Doing this, more samples are present in regions where higher quality topological information is more likely to be obtained and used to improve the identification of ˜ /u1D439 /u1D443 .

Motivated by the PE method and the evolution of the EDAs, is proposed in (CHENG et al., 2015) the IM-MOEA algorithm, which provides a different way of using inverse models. Instead of a method used after the optimization process, the inverse models are inserted internally in the optimization algorithm and then used to create offspring solutions by sampling the objective space. They propose a decomposition of the inverse function, also reducing the number of inverse models, and a reproduction operator who benefits from the inverse model. The purpose of their method is to use the inverse models to increase the density of solutions in the preferred regions at a low computational cost. This approach has gained attention in the literature providing diverse algorithms and variants of the IM-MOEA. The work in (GHOLAMNEZHAD; BROUMANDNIA; SEYDI, 2020) proposes a variant where a random forest feature importance method is used to determine the best assignment of decision variables, improving the training performance of the inverse model. Also, the method proposed in (ZHANG et al., 2020) trains an ANN to perform the grouping strategy for training the inverse model. Different from IM-MOEA, the algorithm IM-MOEA/D proposed by (GEE; TAN; ALIPPI, 2016) is based on decomposition-based MOEA rather than domination-based MOEA. Their algorithm achieves good performance while resolving dynamic multi-objective optimization problems.

## 2.2 Systematic Review

To the best of our knowledge, systematic reviews or mappings that present an overview of the proposed research field of metaheuristics enhanced by machine learning were not found in the literature. Motivated by the lack of secondary studies in the area, a greater understanding in the study of inverse models, and the study of the interception between these areas. We contribute to the literature by providing, in this section, a systematic review of the research field. We followed a well-established protocol based on Kitchenham guidelines (KITCHENHAM, 200») and analyses of 111 papers published in the last ten years. Based on the related works, we discuss some relevant aspects and the finds of different aspects not addressed, such as machine learning techniques used, validation strategies and kind of applications field. Also, we identify new research opportunities and trends.

## 2.2.1 Research Method

In this work, we use a systematic literature review, a methodology to review research results. Based on evidence, which is defined in this context as a synthesis of best quality scientific studies on a specific topic or research question. The systematic literature review assumes that the accumulation of results from scientific experiments is more reliable than the results from expert's opinion. This kind of research was initially developed in medicine and since other domains have adopted this approach, e.g. Criminology, Social policy, Economics, Nursing etc (KITCHENHAM et al., 2009).

Weconductthissystematic literature review following the guidelines proposed by (KITCHENHAM,200») which adapts the methodology to the needs of software engineering researchers. This approach divides the review process into three main phasesȷ Planning the Review, Conducting the Review, Reporting the Review. The first one, Planning the Review, is responsible for creating the protocol used in the research. The second phase, Conducting the Review, performs the planned tasks in the previous phase. The third one, named Reporting the Review, specifies the communication of the research. The last phase resulted in the elaboration of the present work. In this section, we describe the two initial phasesȷ Planning the Review and Conducting the Review.

## 2.2.1.1 Planning the review

This systematic review was motivated by the lack of secondary research in the area. In our preliminary studies, only a few secondary works were found, mainly surveys that outline the specific research area where Machine Learning enhances Metaheuristics algorithms. Instead, the number of primary research in this area has grown due to the motivation in solving expensive and hard optimization problems with multiple objectives. It makes a good opportunity to conduct a systematic review in the area.

## 2.2.1.1.1 Research Questions

Based on our preliminary studies and related works, and considering relevant aspects of the area, we formulated four different research questions (RQs) to be answered by the collected literature.

- RQ1. How can the current research in Machine Learning applied in Metaheuristics be classified, and what is the current state of this classification?
- RQ2. What are the Machine Learning techniques used in Metaheuristic algorithms?
- RQ«. Which strategies were used to validate the algorithm?
- RQ». In which real-world optimization problems were the algorithms applied?

## 2.2.1.1.2 Search String

The selected key search terms in Table 1 were built through an improvement process. First, some initial terms were identified based on our preliminary studies and the reading of the surveys of the area. Then keywords were refined and extended during the search process. In this phase, we use Google Scholar and IEEE Explore to test and refine the search string. We identify that the studies in this area have several terms and keywords to describe their work. For example, the terms "hybridization", "adaptive learning", "incremental learning", "linkage learning", and some variants are present in the studies but do not necessarily identify our aim area. "Hybridization" can refer to the incorporation of any kind of method into the algorithm, not necessarily machine learning into optimization. This led to difficulty finding the key terms, an increase in the search string size, and an increase in the number of the result papers.

Table 1 - The generic search string.

'machine learning' AND ('optimization algorithm' OR metaheuristic OR meta-heuristic OR evolutionary OR genetic) AND (hybrid OR hybridization OR hybridized OR "probabilistic model" OR "adaptive learning" OR "adaptation learning" OR "incremental learning" OR "linkage learning" OR surrogate OR 'response surfaces' OR metamodels OR 'approximate models')

The search was performed during January 2021, and a total of 1.960 papers returned as a result of the execution of the search string on the source list. The steps of the review are shown in Figure 5. Despite the high number of articles found, the result could be greater if we not adopted the exclusion criteria of publications older than ten years. This high number of papers found outlines the lack of existence of a term to represent the Machine Learning enhancing Metaheuristic algorithms. Different terms exist in the literature, and authors use different keywords for representing their studies in the area.

Figure 5 - Systematic review conduction.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Sourceȷ Produced by authors.

From the 1960 papers returned, 219 were removed by duplication, leaving 1.7»1 papers still to be analyzed. In the next phase, we proceeded with a title and abstract screening, achieving 11» papers to perform a full-text screening. Performing the selection criteria, 22 papers were removed, resulting in a total of 92. In these remaining papers, we performed a backward snowballing procedure (WOHLIN, 201») by using the reference list of each selected paper to identify new studies to include that attend our selection criteria. The execution of the snowballing resulted in the addiction of 19 papers to our resulting set. Finally, 111 papers were selected for the next phase, for data extraction.

Concerning the papers removed by the inclusion and exclusion criteria, we found papers that mention the terms of the search string but are out of the scope of this systematic review. For instance, studies that use optimization to support machine learning. We also found hybrid optimization algorithms that use two different kinds of metaheuristics or other techniques instead of machine learning. These kinds of papers and the secondary studies constitute a large number of papers in our search that were removed. Most of the removed primary studies, for example, concerns about the improvement of Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) by optimization algorithms. This specific topic could lead, in future work, to an execution of a systematic review to clarify and answer important questions in the field.

In the last phase, we extracted the data of the selected papers and stored it in a spreadsheet. We consider the title, publication year, venue, and some additional information, to answer our research questions. The results were synthesized, analyzed, and are discussed in the next section.

To answer the second part about the current state of this classification, we divide this subsection into three main parts. First, we analyze the papers by the classification of Time of hybridization. ## 2.2.2.1.1 Time of hybridization

From the 111 resulting papers, the majority, a total of 96 papers, are classified as online and only 15 as off-line, as is summarized in Table 5. The 96 papers that were classified as online dynamically discover the knowledge during the search. This strategy is used when the ML technique used does not violate any restrictions of the optimization problem on the search step, like restrictions on calling the objective function online. And also, when there is no need to incorporate experience knowledge from different executions of the algorithm. This online classification has diverse ML techniques used to learn from different phases of the algorithm that will be analyzed, detailed and discussed further in the following subsection. It is important to note that none of the resulting papers used both online and off-line strategies in combination.

Figure 9 - Number of papers published per year.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Sourceȷ Produced by authors.

From the 15 off-line papers, 1« are implementations of Surrogate-Assisted Evolutionary Algorithms (SAEAs) (JIN, 2011). The SAEAs use computational models, also known as surrogates or metamodels, to approximate the objective function. Mainly motivated by reducing computational time while running the search on expensive problems. The papers in (YIN; TSAI, 2020; PROBST et al., 2019; TANG et al., 2020; PYLE; CHIMEH; RICHMOND, 2019; KACEM et al., 2020; WANG et al., 2018; PARQUE; MIYASHITA, 2017; SAIKIA; RAKSHIT et al., 2020; GHORBEL et al., 2019) have an expensive objective function calculated by a simulator. The result of diverse objective function evaluations is made off-line, before the search begins, by the simulator. In some cases, these simulations are executed separately in parallel or using a supercomputer which restricts function calls to be made online. The SAEA in (GARCÍAORTEGA; GARCÍA-SĂNCHEZ; MERELO-GUERVÓS, 2020), differently from the others, has an objective function that is not expressed mathematically or by simulators. The objective function of this problem is basically a machine-learning model, in particular, a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) (GARDNER; DORLING, 1998), trained from data extracted and processed from film databases before the search starts.

## 2.2.2.1.2 Aim of hybridization

The Aim of hybridization classifies the purpose of the ML enhancement. The combination allows to improve the Efficiency of the algorithm by reducing the search time, or the combination is used to improve the Effectiveness of the algorithm leading to better quality of solutions. Table 6 demonstrates our results based on this classification. From the 70 papers classified as Efficiency, all of them are SAEAs implementations. Mainly due to the nature of this kind of optimization algorithm that is used to reduce the computational time by swapping the expensive objective function by a surrogate. Modeling the objective function can be seen as a supervised ML problem, where the solutions are used to train the model according to the real objective function values. Generally, the use of a metamodel to predict the objective function value is less expensive than using the real objective function, causing an increase in the Efficiency of the algorithm.

We have encountered different ways of enhancing Effectiveness in optimization problems. The studies in (LI et al., 2019b; ZANGARI et al., 2017a; MA et al., 201»; VIRGOLIN et al., 2018; HO et al., 2015; ZANGARI et al., 2017b; WANG et al., 2012; QI et al., 2012; CHENG et al., 2015; SHIM et al., 201«; VIRGOLIN et al., 2017; THIERENS; BOSMAN, 2011) are based on, or variations, of the Estimation of Distribution Algorithm (EDA) (LARRAÑAGA; LOZANO, 2001). Instead of using commonly mutation operators of evolutionary algorithms, it extracts statistical information from selected solutions and builds a posterior probability distribution model to predict promising solutions. implementation plays a crucial role in the results of the algorithm in the search process. So the choice of the PBIL variant can lead to different results in different optimization problems. In (HO et al., 2015), a PBIL implementation for inverse Problems in continuous Space is proposed, where the default implementation is changed to adapt to the optimization problem. Another variant of EDA is proposed by (THIERENS; BOSMAN, 2011), called the Gene-pool Optimal Mixing

Evolutionary Algorithm (GOMEA). This variant mixes EDA with Genetic Algorithm (GA), using a linkage tree (LT) structure to identify the contributions of the variables. Also, another study found in (VIRGOLIN et al., 2017) improves the GOMEA with Genetic Programming (GP), implementing the algorithm GP-GOMEA that requires no parameter specification. In (VIRGOLIN et al., 2018) the GP-GOMEA is adapted to resolve real optimization problems. The GOMEA algorithm and its variants have proven to have good results in real optimization problems and benchmark problems.

Another algorithm found in our results is the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) (HANSEN; OSTERMEIER, 2001). Different from the EDA, it uses a covariance matrix distribution to sample new solutions in the population. In (SANTANA et al., 2012) the CMA-ES is adapted to resolve an optimization problem of classifying Brain Computer Interfaces (BCIs). In (JIANG et al., 2017), the CMA-ES is integrated with the Differential Evolution (DE), a well-known optimization algorithm. It achieves relevant results in benchmarking problems in comparison with other state-of-art algorithms.

Three different papers draw attention by reaching the Efficiency and Effectiveness mutually. In (CUI; TURAN; SAYER, 2012), a reinforcement learning approach is proposed, the method is used to reduce the computation time and also correct the search leading to better solutions. The algorithm MGPMDE proposed by (LIU; KOZIEL; ZHANG, 2016) is a Multi-fidelity/Multilevel/Variable-fidelity Optimization (MFO) method (EL-BELTAGY; KEANE, 1999). This technique uses two ML models, the first one is an approximation model that can be referenced as a surrogate model acting in the improvement of the Efficiency of the metaheuristic. The second one is a low-fidelity model that explores the space leading to an improvement in Effectiveness. The DVL algorithm proposed by (SANTOS; OLIVEIRA; BRITTO, 2019) uses the values found by the objective function evaluations for training a metamodel that predicts promising areas of the search space. The new solutions have better quality enhancing the Effectiveness, and also the algorithm reduces the number of evaluations improving the Efficiency.

## 2.2.2.1.3 Involved Component

The classification of the component involved, based on the taxonomy of EC showed in Figure «, can be seen in Table 7. Only 5 papers were produced to improve the quality of the initial solutions. The main technique used to enhance this component is the opposition-based learning (OBL) (TIZHOOSH, 2005). Basically, it assumes that the initial solutions generated randomly can be far away or not far away from the optimal solutions. If an initial solution is close, it can converge fast to the optimal, but if it is far away, it can lead to a slow convergence of the Pareto Front. To reduce the performance impact due to the convergence of the distant solutions, the OBL proposes to calculate the opposite solutions from the solutions set. These new opposite solutions can lead the search in the opposite direction, improving it by realizing a fast convergence to the optimal set. In (ELAZIZ; OLIVA; XIONG, 2017; WANG; WU; RAHNAMAYAN, 2011;

ALI; SIARRY; PANT, 2012), the OBL shows to enhance different optimization algorithms such as the sine cosine algorithm (SCA) and the DE in many optimization problems. The other 2 papers improve the initial solutions in different ways. In (KACEM et al., 2020), an ANN is used to learning from the experience to improve initial solutions quality. And in (LIU; KOZIEL; ZHANG, 2016), a surrogate is used for validating the searching of initial solutions followed by a clustering method to choose the best group of solutions.

The most found component involved in the resulting papers is the Fitness Evaluation and Selection, mainly due to the high use of SAEAs algorithms. All papers, from a total of 71 are SAEAs implementations or variations that use in some way a metamodel to substitute the expensive objective function. Some of the papers found investigate the enhancement by selecting a portion of the population. In (LIU et al., 201»), the surrogate model is first trained with a population created by Latin Hypercubic Sampling (LHS) (IMAN; DAVENPORT; ZEIGLER, 1980), which generates samples on a multidimensional distribution. After this step, during the generations, the model is trained only with the best solution found. This strategy made it possible to achieve global optimization, support the search, and use a small number of objective function evaluations. Another strategy found for training the surrogate is proposed by (SONG et al., 2018), where it adaptively improves the model by using the Pareto optimal solutions in the local search. These solutions are found by some well-known metrics used in MOPs such as Hypervolume (HV) (WHILE et al., 2006) and Inverted Generational Distance (IGD) (ISHIBUCHI et al., 2015). The HV metric is also used by the SAEA in (AZZOUZ; BECHIKH; SAID, 201»). In the same way as the previous paper, it uses the metric to found the best solutions for train the model. The rest of the SAEAs found are original implementations that change the model used, the optimization problem, or the optimization algorithm. These changes will be detailed analyzed in the next subsections.

A total of «0 papers were found that acts on the component of Population Reproduction and Variation. A representative portion of these papers, 1» from «0, proposed by (LI et al., 2019b; ZANGARI et al., 2017a; MA et al., 201»; SANTANA et al., 2012; VIRGOLIN et al., 2018; HO et al., 2015; ZANGARI et al., 2017b; JIANG et al., 2017; WANG et al., 2012; QI et al., 2012; CHENG et al., 2015; SHIM et al., 201«; VIRGOLIN et al., 2017; THIERENS; BOSMAN, 2011), are variations from the EDA and CMA-ES. Mainly because of the nature of the implementation of these algorithms that uses a probabilistic model and a covariance matrix to learn from the problem and assists the reproduction by predicting promise areas of the solutions that can guide the algorithm to better convergence. The 16 remaining papers apply different strategies to achieve good results, such as clustering, association rules, and supervised tasks to extract the knowledge and enhance the solutions. As an example, the work in (TINÓS, 2020) proposes a new method that uses a radial basis function network (RBFN) to generate crossover masks. The RBFN model is trained as a supervised task where incorporates the knowledge from successful recombination operations in the GA algorithm during the optimization process.

Only 2 papers are found that enhance the Parameter Adaptation of metaheuristics. Both improve the parameters dynamically during the search. The algorithm proposed by (KOTINIS, 201»), uses clustering with fuzzy controllers to adapt the DE parameters. While in (AL-DUOLI

et al., 2018), a decision tree (DT) obtains knowledge based on how the value of the parameter provides good solutions. The last taxonomy to analyze is the Local Search where 5 papers were found that enhances this component. The papers in (ABDESSALEM et al., 2018; GARCÍA et al., 2019; WANG; TANG, 2016; NOURI; DRISS; GHĹDIRA, 2018) use ML to determine where and when to perform a Local Search. This knowledge is extracted from the problem, and different local search operations are proposed to better the divergence and convergence of the algorithm. In (PLASTINO et al., 201») the Local Search component is enhanced by refining solutions within the solution's neighborhood from patterns extracted of elite solutions.

## 2.2.2.2 RQ2. What are the Machine Learning techniques used in Metaheuristic algorithms?

For a better understand and organization, we separate this subsection according to the ML classification by the supervision on training, defined as Supervised Learning, Unsupervised Learning, Semi-supervised Learning, and Reinforcement Learning. The results found are shown in Table 8.

The majority of the papers, a total of 87 uses Supervised Learning to enhance the metaheuristic. The high presence of papers based on the SAEAs algorithm plays an important role in this statistic. In many cases, the metamodel used on an SAEA is modeled as regression, generally because the objective problem is a continuous value. Moreover, the vector of decision variables (or solution) is used as a feature vector for the model. A variety of well-known computational models in the literature are used in this task, including polynomials (also known as response surface methodologies), Gaussian processes (also known as Kriging), neural networks (JIN, 2011). The models and metaheuristics found that were used in more than three papers are shown in Figure 11. Kriging and ANNs were the most used models, and GA, PSO, and DE the metaheuristics for mono-objective and NSGA-II and MOEA/D for multi-objective.

Different strategies and techniques found were used to enhance the prediction of the models. The papers in (ARIAS-MONTAñO; COELLO; MEZURA-MONTES, 2012; AKINSOLU et al., 2019; PENNISI; RUSSO; PAPPALARDO, 2018; HARADA; KAIDAN; THAWONMAS, 2020) differ from other implementations by using surrogates in parallelism. Their results showed that this strategy can benefit some optimization problems. In (YIN; TSAI, 2020; LU; LI; JIN, 201«; WANGetal., 2018; AL-JUBOORI; DATTA, 2019) the ensemble learning (MENDES-MOREIRA et al., 2012) is employed to enhance the prediction performance of the surrogate model. Bagging and boosting are two popular ensemble generation methods, and are also used in these works to outperforms a single surrogate model. The use of cross-validation (BROWNE, 2000) had brought benefits and security to the model selection of the papers in (GARCÍA-ORTEGA; GARCÍA-SĂNCHEZ; MERELO-GUERVÓS, 2020; FARFĂN; CEA, 2021; VOLZ, 2020; TIAN et al., 2019; GHORBEL et al., 2019; TENNE, 2012a). It applies a re-sampling procedure used to evaluate ML models on the data sample, encouraging the selection of a determined model that

The regression task can also be employed in algorithms such as EDAs and CMAEs. The continuous values predicted by the model are used to support the population reproduction and

variation on these algorithms, which allow an understanding of the problem and propose valuable areas of the search space. A different way of using Supervisioned Learning to extract knowledge from the problem are the ones proposed by (CHENG et al., 2015; SANTOS; OLIVEIRA; BRITTO, 2019). In the first paper, an EDA algorithm called IM-MOEA is proposed, where it uses the concept of inverse models, that map all found nondominated solutions from the objective space to the decision space. These models receive as input the values of the objective functions and learn their influence on the variables (or solutions). Like other EDAs, this model is used to predict offspring samples of the decision space. The second paper uses the same concept of modeling inversely. But, different from the EDAs, it uses the model to direct predict solution on the space that approximates to optimum values. Achieving in the evolution process both divergence and convergence.

Another well-known Supervisioned Learning task is the classification. It can be used in the SAEAs to model the constraints, as proposed in (GAO et al., 2020; KUREK; BECKER; LUK, 201«; TENNE, 2012a, 2012a). The classification model is trained in the same manner as the regression, and it is used to predict which solutions satisfy the constraints of the optimization problem. The classification model in (AL-DUOLI et al., 2018) extracts knowledge from the problem, making it possible to predict good solutions that can optimize the algorithm. In (PYLE; CHIMEH; RICHMOND, 2019) the surrogate is created in two different ways, by regression,

and by classification. An ANN is used for both models, and to accomplish the surrogate as a classification task, it uses discrete values of the objective function as the labels in the training step. In their experiments, the classifier achieves better results. A classifier model can also be used to add knowledge to the mutation operator as in (MICHALAK, 2018). The training of the model occurs offline, and during the search, it uses the informed mutation operator. In the proposed operator the classifier is used for determining which bits in a solution vector to consider for mutation.

From the Unsupervised Learning was found a total of 21 papers. Clustering is the most used task from this classification. The papers in (MA et al., 201»; WANG; TANG, 2017; VIRGOLIN et al., 2018; QI et al., 2012) are EDAs or variants that use probabilistic models to guide the solutions in the search space. The clustering is used in these papers to support the algorithm learning method. In (MA et al., 201») for example, the clustering method is used to decompose the MOP into some scalar optimization subproblems. The learning strategy used, called Baldwing learning, is applied in each cluster to find the direction of the cluster in the search space. The algorithm proposed in (QI et al., 2012) uses a similar learning strategy. The clustering method is used to divide the population into K disjoint clusters. And a model is built for each cluster to sampling new solutions at each generation.

Some clustering strategies act directly on the objective modeling by speeding up the search time or reducing the number of evaluations. The cluster method proposed by (LE et al., 2020; LE et al., 2021; LI et al., 2019) evaluates only the solutions closest to the cluster center, the objective function value of the remaining solutions is calculated by an approximation to their distance to the evaluated solutions. These algorithms differ in the calculation strategy used to infer the objective function values of new solutions. Clustering can also be used to perform different kinds of searches. In (GARCÍA et al., 2019) a Db-Scan cluster operator is used to create different groups of the population. In each group is executed a different approach of search, based on the knowledge extract from the group.

Association rule learning is another kind of unsupervised learning task. We have found » papers that use association rules to enhance metaheuristics. The approaches found in (ALDUOLI et al., 2018; WANG; YIN, 2018) uses association rules to enhance the effectiveness of the algorithm. Data Mining techniques are used to discover patterns associated with good solutions. This knowledge is used during the search to improve the convergence to better solutions. In (ZHANG; SHAFI; ABBASS, 201»), instead of search rules on the solutions, the association rules are discovered from optimal areas of the design space. The knowledge extracted improves the convergence of the algorithm by leading it to search for optimal areas. A new design of local search is proposed by (PLASTINO et al., 201»), where after a predefined number of iterations the local search is conducted by association rules extracted from elite solutions.

We have found only one paper that contributes by using a Semi-supervised Learning approach. In (SUN et al., 201«) the Cotraining Algorithm for Semi-supervised Learning (CSSL)

is used to handle the inherent uncertainties in fitness assignment by human users, where, interval-based fitness values are assigned to individuals. Also, only one paper found that uses Reinforcement Learning. Already noticed in previous sections, the algorithm proposed by (CUI; TURAN; SAYER, 2012) uses Q-learning (WATKINS; DAYAN, 1992), a model-free reinforcement learning technique. That uses the predicted Q-value calculation to replace the expensive objective function evaluation and also to improve the operation of the selection of offspring solutions, leading to a correction on the search direction and improving the quality of the solutions.

## 2.2.2.3 RQ3. Which strategies were used to validate the algorithm?

This question is to determine the validating techniques used to investigate the performance of metaheuristics algorithms enhanced by ML. The analyses performed on the optimization algorithms are mostly quantitative via validation metrics like mean error, standard deviation, and co-relations. Researchers have most commonly used benchmark test functions to validate the quality of optimization procedures. Details about these functions are available in (MOLGA; SMUTNICKI, 2005). Researchers also use state-of-art metaheuristics from literature for comparison with the new algorithm.

In most papers, the researchers have commonly used well-known benchmark test functions. Table 9 shows which kind of benchmark was used in each paper found. Some of them found in the papers are ZDT (ZITZLER; DEB; THIELE, 2000), DTLZ (DEB et al., 2002b), CF (ZHANG et al., 2008), F functions from the CEC 2005 (SUGANTHAN et al., 2005), the test functions in (JAMIL; YANG, 201«), and WFG (HUBAND et al., 2005). Beyond the test functions, some researchers used problem-specific benchmark problems, such as the benchmark data for FJSSP in (CHAMBERS; BARNES, 1996; DAUZÈRE-PĹRÈS; PAULLI, 1997), benchmark instances for PFSP (MINELLA; RUIZ; CIAVOTTA, 2008), CMT benchmark problems for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), and the Mazda benchmark problem of Multiple Car Structures (KOHIRA et al., 2017).

While comparing the performance with other metaheuristics, the PSO and NSGA-II are the most used with 10 appearances each, as shown in Figure 12. The GA, MOEA/D and DE, appears right after with 8, 7 and 6 references each. If we use the nature of the metaheuristic for comparison, the algorithms based on GA takes the lead, since the NSGA-II is based on GA for problems with multiple objectives and the combination of these two algorithms appears in 15 papers.

Diverse validation criteria were used for comparison. These include mean, median, best, worst, and standard deviation of the objective function values or other metrics, such as the Hypervolume and Normalized Hypervolume, GD and IGD, c-metric, and e-indicator. Other than comparing with these methods, some statistical analysis techniques have also been utilized, such as the Wilcoxon SignedRank test, Friedman's test, t-test (ZIMMERMAN, 1997),
