## 2.2.2.4 RQ4. In which real-world optimization problems the algorithms were applied?

Some aspects of real-world optimization problems make them very challenging. Some examples are the presence of an enormous number of local optima within the search space, the high number of the decision variable, and an expensive objective function. In this subsection we describe some aspects of these problems.

Most of the real-world optimization problems found are related to the set of problems that optimizes some aspect of the Machine Learning algorithm. The approaches found in the studies were used to optimizes the ML data preprocessing step, the ANN architecture, and the hyperparameters of the algorithm. Data preprocessing is a key step in a data mining application or ML process, many problems of this step, such as feature selection or instance selection can be modeled as an optimization problem (LE et al., 2020). In (LE et al., 2020; LE et al., 2021) they proposed optimization algorithms for the problem of undersampling in imbalanced classification problems. The use of advanced techniques and algorithms to automatically design the architecture of ANNs is a problem that has drawn attention in the literature, and some studies are achieving good results. The papers in (GATOPOULOS et al., 2020; ZHOU; JIN; DING, 2020; XIE et al., 2021; MAHESWARANATHAN et al., 2019; STOEAN, 2020) are studies found in our review that specifically deal with tuning the architecture of ANNs. Another way of increasing the performance of an ML model involves the tuning of hyperparameters. These hyperparameters

Figure 1« Metrics used for validation with at least three papers.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Sourceȷ Produced by authors.

depend on the learning algorithm, which causes the characteristics of the search problem to depend on the learning technique. In (PENG et al., 2019; MARTINEZ-CANTIN, 2018) are proposed algorithms that cover the hyperparameters improvement in general.

A set of problems found requires the use of expensive simulators. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) gives simulations to evaluate the performance of a given structure. These simulations can take over ten-hour to perform one calculation (JIN, 2005). The problems in (WANG et al., 2018; TENNE, 2012b; AZZOUZ; BECHIKH; SAID, 201»; TENNE, 2012a; ARIASMONTAñO; COELLO; MEZURA-MONTES, 2012; GHORBEL et al., 2019; MARTINEZCANTIN, 2018) aim to resolve aerodynamic design problems, principally related to the shape and design of airfoils and wings. In some cases as in (TANG et al., 2020), the aerodynamic of the entire underwater vehicle's shape is an expensive problem to be optimized, which also makes use of the CFD simulation. In some problems as in (PARK, 2019), the simulation is used for computing the gas cyclone shape to evaluate the separation performance, separation efficiency, and pressure drop. The last problem found that uses CFD is the one proposed by (PROBST et al., 2019). The need for engine simulation makes use of CFD for modeling the combustion in the system. The Variable-fidelity Electromagnetic Model (EM) is another kind of computationally expensive simulation that is widely used in antenna array design optimization (KOZIEL; LEIFSSON; YANG, 201»). The papers in (WU; WANG; HONG, 2020; CAO et al., 2019; LIU; KOZIEL;

ZHANG, 2016; LIU et al., 201») resolve this design problem with different surrogates strategies and achieve good results in their experiments.

Different areas have been studying and developing methods to resolve the scheduling problems (TAILLARD, 199«). Which basically is the allocation of a job to a machine in a determined time. This type of problem can be subdivided into different problems. We have encountered in (WANG et al., 2012; LI et al., 2019b; NOURI; DRISS; GHĹDIRA, 2018) approaches to resolve the Flexible Job-shop Scheduling Problem (FJSSP). Different from the classical job shop scheduling problem (JSSP), FJSSP is more general because the sequence of operations is allowed to be assigned to any machine of a given set instead of a prescribed one (LI et al., 2019b). In (WANG; TANG, 2017), the problem to resolve is a flowshop scheduling problem. Which is a strict of the JSSP where there is a strict order to perform the operations.

## 2.2.3 Research agenda

This section describes some of the related but potential areas of research that may build future literature. But before discussing the trends and research opportunities, we give a summary of the results found in this systematic review as well as the gaps identified.

## 2.2.3.1 Summary

As mentioned in the previous section, a total of 111 works were found. None of them presents a novel kind of enhancement that was not in the taxonomies explained in our related works. The majority of these papers are based on SAEAs and EDAs, two different kinds of metaheuristic algorithms enhanced by ML. Based on the classification of when the knowledge is extracted, from the 111 papers, 96 papers use online strategies. Based on the impact of the enhancement, 70 papers use the Efficiency strategy. By the Involved Component, 72 papers enhance the Fitness Evaluation and Selection step. Supervised learning was the most found kind of machine learning problem, a total of 87 papers, most of them modeled as regression. Over half of the papers, precisely 60 studies, do not use benchmark instances to validate the problem, and only 1» papers use real benchmark instances. We found several types of real-world applications optimized by these papers, some of them areȷ enhance machine learning problems, aerodynamic design problems, and scheduling problems.

## 2.2.3.2 Gaps

During our research, we could identify some gaps in the primary studies. To prove the validity of a newly designed metaheuristic algorithm, the researchers employ some performance validation criteria. These criteria are used to compare to well-known algorithms to prove the effectiveness of an algorithm. The gaps found in these studies are concerning to the validation criteria used in their studiesȷ

1. The comparison with state-of-the-art optimization algorithms is a common practice in the literature to validate a new algorithm implementation. Despite that, we identify in the resulting paper set that in the 111 studies, «2 don't compare with state-of-the-art algorithms, only validate their new algorithm with different settings in a specific optimization problem;
2. In general, theoretically evaluating the performance of an optimization algorithm can be a hard task. That is why artificially designed benchmark functions have been widely used. Besides facilitating the experimentation process and prove its performance in different situations, these functions allow the easy reproduction of the experiment by other researchers. In our resulting papers, 60 don't apply the algorithm in a benchmark test function, making it difficult to simulate and compare the presented results;
3. «. Statistical tests have become a widespread technique in computational intelligence, and several different test kind has proven to be robust to be used in metaheuristic (DERRAC et al., 2011). But only 26 papers make use of statistical tests to improve the evaluation process of the new method.
4. ». The last gap found is relative to the machine learning validation. Only a few papers compare the performance of different models or techniques. Most papers apply well-known methods that have a good performance in a certain kind of algorithm, such as Kriging and ANNs for metamodeling.

These validations gaps make us identify the need to improve the experimentation phase with robust validation criteria in the papers found in our review.

## 2.2.3.3 Trends and research opportunities

Based on the results found in this review, we observed some research gaps and limitations. In the next subsections, we discuss the research opportunities found, and present some trends in the investigation of the field.

## 2.2.3.3.1 SAEAs

Despite several advantages of using MOEAs on expensive objective functions, there are some important limitations while dealing with it, such as the relatively high number of objective function evaluations. By this, there is a motivation in the research field to find different approaches to deal with the problem. In (COELLO et al., 2020) surrogates have already been pointed as a trend in this area. In our systematic review, we identified several different approaches of SAEAs that obtained a good performance in this kind of problem, but this research field stills a challenge for the area. There is a lack of experimentation and comparison of the performance of different metamodels in diverse optimization applications. Also, some new strategies proposed need to be strongly validated in benchmark instances and in real-world applications. Most SAEAs normally

can handle expensive optimization problems with a low number of variables efficiently, but when the number of the dimensions increases many challenges appears to the algorithm. The use of machine learning methods such as principal component analysis and feature selection can benefit the surrogate performance in such problems (GARCÍA et al., 2019). Only a few papers, proposed in (LIU et al., 2012; DAI; WANG; YANG, 2020; TIAN et al., 2020b), address this problem and obtains the benefits in applying ML methods in problems with a high number of dimensions. Due to the large number of methods that use or extend SAEAs, we identify that a systematic review or systematic mapping that analyzes this area can be of great importance to the optimization field.

## 2.2.3.3.2 EDAs

Algorithms based on probabilistic modeling have been successfully applied for solving different optimization problems. We have found in the resulting papers diverse variants of EDAs with different design strategies to successfully obtain knowledge from the problem to enhance the convergence and divergence of the Pareto front. We understand that the trend in this area relies on continuing to explore and experiment with different models and novel designs to improve the knowledge during the search. Also, validate the performance of the proposed EDA in different real-world optimization problems to understand if the strategy is generally sufficient to be used in any kind of problem. As in the same manner with the SAEAs algorithms, a systematic review and/or systematic mapping for EDAs could also lead to future work. The researchers can identify unique knowledge from these papers that could not be identified in our research due to the scope covered in this review.

## 2.2.3.3.3 Explore Machine learning techniques

As also stated by (WANG et al., 2018), the use of different and more advanced machine learning techniques could be employed to improve the performance of the algorithm. The first example is ensemble learning, which is a method that explores the combination of several models. This combination can enhance the performance of the algorithm as shown in (YIN; TSAI, 2020; LU; LI; JIN, 201«; WANG et al., 2018; AL-JUBOORI; DATTA, 2019). We identify that more exploration of this technique to improve the results could be a trend to research. Other methods such as data preprocessing, deep learning, transfer learning, and other advanced machine learning techniques could be also deep studied to enhancing metaheuristics algorithms.

By the ML classification, some areas that obtain good results could be the target for further research. Semi-supervised Learning, for example, that was found in only one paper in our research, is able to enhance the performance of the surrogate-assisted algorithm when there is uncertainty in the fitness evaluations or when there is data paucity in the optimization problem (SUN et al., 201«). Also, Reinforcement Learning was present in only one paper, and as we detailed, obtained better performance in terms of both speed and final results. More studies in

these areas could provide more knowledge to the research field as well as identifying new design alternatives in these classifications.

We have identified in this systematic review several novel methods, based on different ML techniques, that have been successfully applied in different components of the metaheuristic. But this also raises a question about the impact that this method has on different components of the algorithm. Experiments with that purpose were not identified in the studies. The understanding of the impact of the method on different components could lead to the validation of robust methods and also the discovery of new approaches and interest areas. An attractive research line is to investigate the combination of more than one ML method in the same metaheuristic. The approaches in (LI et al., 2019; AL-DUOLI et al., 2018; GAO et al., 2020; PARQUE; MIYASHITA, 2017; LIU; KOZIEL; ZHANG, 2016; TENNE, 2012a), uses more than one method in different areas or in the same component but as support for the other technique. Increasing the performance of the algorithm in comparison if only one method was adopted.

## 2.2.3.3.4 Knowledge Discovery

During the studies of the resulting papers, we have identified a large set of works that increase the efficiency by using surrogates and a smaller portion that enhances the effectiveness with EDAs and variants. Within this group, principally the one who enhances the effectiveness, some of these papers call our attention to the results found and the opening of new research possibilities. Their studies provide different approaches for discovering forms of knowledge during the search process. An example is the Baldwing learning strategy proposed by (QI et al., 2012) and the deterministic Markov decision process, Q-learning proposed by (CUI; TURAN; SAYER, 2012).

Another interesting learning approach found is the inverse modeling. First proposed by (GIAGKIOZIS; FLEMING, 2012) as an approach to increase the number of non-dominant solutions, that maps the values of the objective functions to decision variables, in an inverse manner as the surrogates models. In this systematic review, we have encountered two approaches that use the inverse model that differs from the one proposed by (CHENG et al., 2015; SANTOS; OLIVEIRA; BRITTO, 2019). The knowledge extracted from the model in these works allowed a better final quality of the solutions, improving the performance of the metaheuristic. This knowledge extracted from an inverse model can be further well explored in further research. And also, the works found opened new paths for research in the area. First, the method proposed by (CHENG et al., 2015) can be improved with different approaches in finding the better samples for training the model, choose the better combination of models, and improving the generation of the new solutions. From the method in (SANTOS; OLIVEIRA; BRITTO, 2019), it can be further improved as a method for providing solutions next to the Pareto front in combination with an MOEA, taking advantage of the strengths of each algorithm. In these two methods, experimentation of different ML models and techniques could find the best approach to enhance

the performance of the algorithm. We believe that the enhancement of the effectiveness of metaheuristics with these open research areas brings a new trend to the studied field.

## 2.2.4 Threats to validity

In this section, we describe the possible threats to the validity of our systematic review. According to (WOHLIN et al., 2012), four types of threats to the validity of experimental research must be analyzed. We conduct the remaining of this section motivated by this classification.

## 2.2.4.1 Construct validity

This validity is concerned with the relation between the theory and the observation (WOHLIN et al., 2012). One possible threat to the construct validity is the exclusion of relevant studies. That is why, it is related to the search string, research question, and databases used. Focus on these steps is important to not miss important studies in the review. Because of this, in this systematic review, we aim to construct the search string as general as possible, even if the size of the search result increased. But we confirm that the search string will coverage the studied field. We also make use of a control group of relevant papers about machine learning enhancing metaheuristics algorithms to validate the search string, described in the subsection 2.1.«

The research questions may not address all aspects of the field. To reduce this threat, we formulated research questions that cover the main elements of the field found in the related works. To mitigate the threats related to the choice of databases, we used multiple databases to avoid eventual limitations implied by a particular database. Databases are selected by considering their relevance to the computer science area. Only one database searched did not return papers published in important venues of the field.

## 2.2.4.2 Internal validity

This validity refers to a causal relationship between treatment and outcome (WOHLIN et al., 2012). When the researcher is investigating if one factor affects other, there is a risk that the investigated factor is also affected by a third factor. If the researcher is not aware of the third factor it could create a threat to the internal validity. To reduce this threat, we were guided by the inclusion and exclusion criteria, applying them when analyzing the papers. Beyond that, we performed a snowballing reading in the selected studies and included relevant studies. Meetings were made between the researchers to discuss doubts in data extraction and re-readings were performed to clear existing doubts. Also, we did not include grey literature in our research, due to the possibility to arise a threat to internal validity from unpublished research that had undesired outcomes or proprietary literature that is not made available.

## 2.2.4.3 External validity

This validity is concerned with the generalization of results outside the scope of the study (WOHLIN et al., 2012). We can relate it to what it is possible to extend to generalize the findings, and to what extent the findings are of interest to other people outside the scope of the review. To reduce this threat the adoption of a review protocol helped to achieve a representative set of studies that have a greater extent. Also, the number of researchers found, from different countries and a wide list of application areas make us believe that the finds in our review can be generalized to many different areas.

## 2.2.4.4 Conclusion validity

This validity refers to problems that affect the ability to draw the correct conclusions from the paper (WOHLIN et al., 2012). One possible threat to this validity is the failure in applying a good quality assessment and data extraction. To minimize this threat, we explicitly define inclusion and exclusion criteria that are detailed enough to provide an assessment of how we reached the final set of papers for analysis. To assess the consistency of data extraction, the spreadsheet generated from the extraction was reviewed and analyzed several times to maintain its validity. Another threat is related to the ability to replicate this review and obtain the same results. We believe that using the protocol and the details presented in our conduction satisfies this threat, making it possible to be replicated following the steps provided and using the search string.

## Validating DVL Performance

As reviewed in chapter 2, the use of machine learning methods to enhance metaheuristics has called the attention of the research literature. The main reason is the ability to handle hard optimization problems such as MOPs and MaOPs. SAEAs have been used to metamodeling expensive objective functions and are capable of achieving good results in improving the performance of optimization algorithms. Motivated by the use of surrogates, some researchers propose inverse modeling, which maps the objective function to the decision variables. The application of this method demonstrated that inferences of Pareto's optimum front can be achieved by the use of machine learning models. Recently, the DVL algorithm has been proposed, where the inverse model is used to directly estimate the Pareto front, differently from the previous studies. To advance in the improvement of the algorithm, it is necessary to validate the following hypothesisȷ inverse models can have good performance in estimating the Pareto optimal set. We believe that the research done in (SANTOS; OLIVEIRA; BRITTO, 2019) needs to be experimentally improved to confirm this hypothesis. Also, we need to validate the DVL as an algorithm for Many-objective Optimization in comparison with a state-of-the-art MOEA, such as the NSGA-III. For this reason, in this chapter, we propose to test the inverse model and the DVL algorithm in a larger set of experiments in MOP and MaOPs, using a variety set of benchmark functions and machine learning models for validation.

In the following sections, we describe the DVL algorithm, present the benchmark test problems used in the experiments as well as the learning models used to learn the decision variables. Two different test configurations are described and analyzed. The first one is called the regression experiment, and the second is the optimization experiment. The parameter settings and the performance indicators used in each test are described at the beginning of each test subsection.

## 3.1 Decision Variable Learning algorithm (DVL)

The Decision Variable Learning algorithm (SANTOS; OLIVEIRA; BRITTO, 2019) aims to use machine learning models to generate an approximated Pareto optimal set using information from samples of the objective space and a set of reference points. Differently from the Pareto Estimation (PE), the DVL is not a method used after the MOEA, instead, it is an algorithm that uses the inverse model approach into the algorithm to solve multi-objective problems. Although in the elaboration of the DVL the authors were not aware of the studies relative to the inverse model, the DVL has the theoretical basis of the PE method. But, instead of using the inverse model to increase the number of non-dominated solutions, the DVL directly infers an approximation of the Pareto optimal set.

DVL is based on three main steps, the first one is the creation of an initial sample dataset, that contains solutions with their respective objective functions. This initial sample generation is provided by the LHS method, which generates well-distributed samples over the search space. The second step is the training of the inverse method, a machine learning model is used for this purpose, which is fed with the dataset generate previously. The idea that supports this modeling is that, for continuous MOPs, it can be deduced from the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality conditions that the Pareto optimal set is a piecewise continuous in the decision variables (GIAGKIOZIS; FLEMING, 201»). Depending on the machine learning model, /u1D440 /u1D45B models are created, and each one estimates only one variable, so each solution generated in this process will be composed of variables estimated by different models. Another strategy is to use only one model /u1D440 that can be used to estimate the entire decision variable set. In the original implementation (SANTOS; OLIVEIRA; BRITTO, 2019), /u1D440 /u1D45B linear Ridge models are used, however, in our experiments we use a variety of models with different strategies to validate the impacts that different models have on learning decision variables. The last step is the prediction of new solutions next to the Pareto optimal set. The objectives set used as input for this step is the same as the PE method, which is based on the method in (DAS; DENNIS, 1996), that places points on a normalized hyper-plane equally inclined to all objective axes and has an intercept of one on each axis. The algorithm was projected to work iteratively, where, at each iteration, the training of the machine learning model and prediction of a new population is executed. These steps are performed using a set of solutions that is incremented at each iteration.

The algorithm was projected to work iteratively, where, at each iteration, the training of the machine learning model and prediction of a new population is executed. These steps are performed using a set of solutions that is incremented at each iteration. The pseudocode of the DVL is described in Algorithm 1.

As shown in the algorithm, the process is started from the creation of an initial dataset /u1D443 with several solutions from the LHS. be composed of variables estimated by different models. This training and estimation phase is repeated until reaches a stop condition. In the original implementation (SANTOS; OLIVEIRA; BRITTO, 2019), the linear Ridge model is used, however, in our experiments we use a variety of models to validate the impacts that different models have on learning decision variables.

The purpose of this iterative approach is to improve the quality of the dataset and thereby improve future estimations since the dataset will have solutions closer to the reference points. The details of each step, defined in Algorithm 1, will be further discussed in the next subsections.

## 3.1.1 Dataset and environment variables preparation

Initially, on line 2, the solution set /u1D443 is created. This initial set can be interpreted as a dataset with /u1D45A + /u1D45B columns and /u1D458 lines, where /u1D45A is the number of objectives of the problem, /u1D45B is the number of variables, and /u1D458 is the size of the initial solutions set. Therefore, each row of this dataset corresponds to a pair ( /u1D44B , /u1D44C ) , where /u1D44B = [ /u1D465 1 , /u1D465 2 , ..., /u1D465 /u1D45A ] is the vector of objectives, /u1D44C = [ /u1D466 1 , /u1D466 2 , ..., /u1D466 /u1D45B ] is the vector of decision variables and /u1D465 /u1D456 = /u1D453 /u1D456 ( /u1D44C ) , where /u1D453 /u1D456 is the objective

function /u1D456 . Each model will use the subset of data that will contain the pairs ( /u1D44B , /u1D466 /u1D456 ) . In the original paper (SANTOS; OLIVEIRA; BRITTO, 2019), this initial dataset can be obtained in two waysȷ from sampling techniques or using individuals generated during the execution of an MOEA. However, it is demonstrated that the use of the LHS (IMAN; DAVENPORT; ZEIGLER, 1980) achieved better results on the DVL algorithm. The purpose of this methodology is to create a set of solutions that explore the entire space of variables and thereby explore all objective space. After generating the initial dataset, on line «, each solution is evaluated using the real objective function and added to the /u1D443 set.

After the dataset creation, some environment variables need to be initialized to enter the iterative process. First, the reference points set /u1D445 /u1D443 that is used to estimate the new solutions are created in the function GenerateReferencePoints() based on the method in (DAS; DENNIS, 1996). The reference points created by this method are placed on a normalized hyperplane which is also inclined to each objective and has an intersection on each axis. In a problem with « objectives, for example, the reference points are created on a triangle with the apex at (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), and (0, 0, 1), with several points evenly divided within its area. Before the iterative process begins it is necessary to create two variables to maintain the best set of solutions and the hypervolume of this solution set, the /u1D443 /u1D44F /u1D452 /u1D460 /u1D461 and /u1D43B/u1D449 /u1D44F /u1D452 /u1D460 /u1D461 respectively.

## 3.1.2 Iterative process

After the initial generation of the data and preparation of the environment variables, the iterative process is started. This process aims to train models of machine learning and from these models, to estimate solutions. The idea behind this proposal is that, for each decision variable of the problem, models will be used to learn the relationship between objective functions and the decision variable and from the information learned by the models estimate solutions that generate points in the space of objectives close to reference points that are considered optimal.

Aset /u1D443 /u1D45F /u1D45D is initialized, on line 8, to maintain the new solutions generated at each iteration. Line 9 begins the process to estimate the points closer to the reference points, the following approach was definedȷ for each reference point, /u1D45B models will be used, these /u1D45B models will be trained with a dataset that contains the solutions closest to the reference point /u1D45F . Lines 10 and 11 correspond to two main methods of the algorithm described in the next subsectionsȷ

## 3.1.2.1 FindClosestSolutions

To train the models it was defined in (SANTOS; OLIVEIRA; BRITTO, 2019) that different datasets would be used. These datasets are subsets of the entire solutions set generated, where the solutions of each subset correspond to the solutions closest to the reference point that the model should estimate. The function receives as parameters the reference point /u1D45F , the entire solutions set /u1D443 and the size /u1D450 of the closest solutions subset. The result of this function is the subset /u1D443 /u1D45B /u1D452 /u1D44E/u1D45F with the solutions closest to the reference point /u1D45F . The distance measure for this

calculus is the Euclidean norm between /u1D45F and the points in /u1D443 . The motivation behind choosing this approach is that in many problems certain regions of the objective space are difficult to achieve. So training models with the whole set of solutions located in these regions is not very effective because the models will be biased to estimate solutions in more common regions.

## 3.1.2.2 TrainModels

In this step, for a problem with /u1D45B variables, /u1D45B supervised learning models will be used, where each model /u1D440 /u1D456 , for 0 &lt; /u1D456 &lt; = /u1D45B , will learn the function /u1D454 /u1D456 ( /u1D44C ) = /u1D465 /u1D456 , where Y is a vector of objectives and /u1D465 /u1D456 is the i-th decision variable of solution /u1D44B , such that Y is the objective vector of solution X. The models will use the set of closest points /u1D443 /u1D45B /u1D452 /u1D44E/u1D45F for training. In this work, several models will be further compared in the experiments section to analyze the impacts of different models in learning decision variables. On line 12 a solution /u1D460 is predicted from the reference point /u1D45F defined as /u1D460 = [ /u1D440 1 ( /u1D45F ) , /u1D440 2 ( /u1D45F ) , ..., /u1D440 /u1D45B ( /u1D45F )] . On line 1« the new solution /u1D460 is added to the /u1D443 /u1D45F /u1D45D set. After the new solutions are generated based on the reference points through the for loop, the solutions from /u1D443 /u1D45F /u1D45D are evaluated and the normalized Hypervolume /u1D43B/u1D449 of these solutions is calculated. If this hypervolume value is better than the best hypervolume encountered /u1D43B/u1D449 /u1D44F /u1D452 /u1D460 /u1D461 then the best solution set is saved and maintained on the /u1D443 /u1D44F /u1D452 /u1D460 /u1D461 variable.

In the end, if a stop condition is not reached, the population is added to the set of solutions /u1D443 , and the process is repeated, otherwise, the best population /u1D443 /u1D44F /u1D452 /u1D460 /u1D461 generated during the process is returned as a result. The proposal of adding the individuals on the population /u1D443 was used considering that the new individuals generated can add information that did not exist in the original dataset since the trend is that the individuals generated will be closer to the reference points. The stop condition of the DVL is reached when a maximum number of iterations is exceeded or when the difference between the hypervolume of the population generated in the current iteration and the hypervolume of the population generated in the previous iteration is less than a value /u1D716 .

In the DVL experiments, the algorithm is tested in comparison with NSGA-III in problems with « and 10 objectives. In some of these problems, the DVL performs better than the NSGA-III, mainly in situations where the number of evaluations was small. This makes us believe that further exploration of the algorithm can lead to better results and open research areas for investigation. We found that some limitations of the algorithm can be better explored. Firstly, it is well-known that different ML models could lead to better results in different function approximations, it is needed to explore the performance of different models and machine learning techniques in estimate the Pareto optimal set in a wide variety of MOPs and MaOPs. Secondly, the strategy used for choosing the decision variables for training each model may vary according to the problem in question. In (CHENG et al., 2015) for example, it uses random grouping to increase the probability of allocating correlated decision variables into different sub-problems.

Thirdly, we also note that the iterations of the algorithm do not always lead to improvement

of the Pareto set, there is a lack of an exploratory process inside the algorithm to search for neighboring regions. Without this process the algorithm tends to become stagnant after a certain number of iterations, resulting in approximate hypervolume values. Attached to that we verify that the use of the reference point as input for the inverse model achieves good results in the initial iterations but it tends to lose strength because it does not represent the shape of the real PF. Finally, the calculation of the hypervolume of a front inside the iteration process makes the algorithm have an expensive computational complexity, exponential in the number of objectives in the worst case, as demonstrated in (WHILE et al., 2006).

## 3.2 Experiments and Results

In this section, we evaluate the DVL algorithm through empirical experiments that have two main motiv ationsȷ first, it is necessary to validate the possibility to learn decision variables from objective functions, for this, we propose the Regression experiment. Secondly, in the Optimization experiment, we validate the impact that different learning models have on the algorithm. Also, we validate the DVL as an algorithm for Many-objective Optimization in comparison with a state-of-the-art MOEA, the NSGA-III.

In our experiments, we used the first seven test problems from the DTLZ benchmark test suite (DEB et al., 2005)ȷ DTLZ1 to DTLZ7, which are multiobjective problems for optimization that have different configurations and shapes of the Pareto-optimal front. The problems are parameterized from a variable /u1D458 , where /u1D458 = /u1D45B -/u1D45A + 1 , being /u1D45B the number of variables and /u1D45A the number of objectives of the problem. Two different instances were defined for each problem, one with « objectives and 12 variables and the other with 10 objectives and 12 variables. By the DTLZ definition, the complexity of 10 objectives is lower than the complexity of « objectives. But this variation of the objective number allows the identification of the influence of the objectives in the learning model. In initial experiments, the variation in decision variables showed no impact on algorithm performance, so the number of variables is set to 12 in both cases. All the algorithms in the experiments were subjected to the same conditions, and our experiments aim to make a comparative analysis between them.

Two different test configurations are described and analyzed. The first one is called the regression experiment, and the second is the optimization experiment. The parameter settings and the performance indicators used in each test are described at the beginning of each test subsection. In all experiments, the algorithms are executed independently 20 times for each configuration. Different visual comparisons are used to better demonstrate the results of each experiment. In both experiments, the Friedman's test followed by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test is adopted to compare the results between each configuration of the experiments with a value of 0.05 of the significance level. The best results in the following tables will be highlighted in bold, if more than one value is highlighted in bold it means that there is no statistically significant

difference between the result and the best value. In the default implementation of the DVL algorithm, /u1D45B models are created to estimate each decision variable. Different from the strategy used in (GIAGKIOZIS; FLEMING, 201») where a single model is used to estimate the entire decision variable set. Because of the dependence between the input and the outputs that can occur in optimization problems, the two strategies are applied in our experiments.

## 3.2.1 Learning Models

A set of different regression machine learning models are used in our experiments to evaluate the impacts of these models in learning the decision variables. The Linear model, an artificial neural network, more precisely a multilayer perceptron (MLP) (GARDNER; DORLING, 1998), a random forest regression (RFR) (SVETNIK et al., 200«), and a support vector regression (SVR) (SMOLA; SCHÖLKOPF, 200»). Each one has unique characteristics that make them perform well in certain types of problems. The implementation and the parameters of each model were defined by Scikit-learn (PEDREGOSA et al., 2011), a python module that integrates a wide range of state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms. Different from the default implementation of each model in the Scikit-learn, the parameters used are described in Table 10. The values of the parameters described were the best found by experimentation in the diverse problems of the benchmark test suit.

With few exceptions, Machine Learning algorithms don't perform well when the input has numerical attributes with very different scales (GĹRON, 2019). It is the case of the objective values of the DTLZ benchmark test suit. Therefore, for each model was used the standardization

transformation which is an algorithm of feature scaling (KIM et al., 2018). The standardization subtracts the mean value (so standardized values always have a zero mean), and then it divides by the variance so that the resulting distribution has unit variance. This transformation causes a better performance in our experiments.

To validate and analyze the strategy of using one model to predict the entire decision variable set or using one model to each decision variable, in our experiments, we applied the multioutput regression in the models to obtain knowledge from the dependence between inputs and outputs. The exception is the SVR model, which implementation in Scikit-learn does not have support to multioutput regression. The models with this strategy are denoted with an "MO" before the model name in our results.

## 3.2.2 Regression Experiment

The first experiment is motivated to answer if it is possible to learn decision variables from objective functions. The task of understanding and predicting the variables of the DTLZ benchmark test problems can be classified as supervised learning since we have the input and output for the learning algorithm and can be classified as a regression task since we want to predict a numerical value. This experiment is based on two phasesȷ training and testing. First, the model is trained by the execution of the DVL algorithm. The generated samples and modeling strategy follow the default flow of the algorithm. Secondly, in the testing step, a subset of the Pareto-optimal front of each DTLZ problem serves as input to the model for prediction. The DTLZ benchmark test suit allows the generation of the Pareto-optimal front of each problem analytically. The key idea of this experiment is to analyze if the inverse modeling of the DVL algorithm can correctly predict the optimal set of a problem. In a real optimization problem, the optimal front is unknown, but the purpose of this experiment is to validate the inverse modeling strategy trained with solutions far from the optimal front.

The overall workflow of the regression experiment is demonstrated in Figure 1». Each model in this experiment is trained with an initial number of solutions generated through the LHS algorithm. The size of the initial sample solutions is defined as 10000. For each DTLZ problem, approximately 5000 solutions of the Pareto-optimal front were generated for the experiment. The values of these Pareto-optimal front were obtained through the execution of diverse MOEAs without restriction and a post-processing routine implemented to eliminate duplicates and choose a diversified set of solutions. The objective function values of these generated solutions are computed and passed as input for each model to predict the decision variables. The predicted values of each model are evaluated to the objective space. The mean-squared error (MSE) (WANG; BOVIK, 2009) metric is used to make empirical comparisons between the results of each model. The MSE is the average squared difference between the predicted optimal front and the Paretooptimal front values. The model with the lower MSE value was more successful in predicting decision variables.

It can be observed in the DTLZ2 problem with « objectives that the two areas approach both in terms of convergence and divergence.

In all charts, the models used achieved a high convergence, i.e. the values found are very close to the ideal. In the majority of the problems the predicted values obtained have performed well in both divergence and convergence values. In these problems, the shape of the region formed by the predicted values is quite similar to the shape of the Pareto-optimal front, for example, DTLZ2 and DTLZ7 problems, Figures 16 and 21, respectively. In Figures 15a, and 17a, respectively, DTLZ1, and DTLZ« problems, the models could not find all parts of the Pareto-optimal for « objectives. It occurred mainly due to the fact of the high search space presented in these problems. Also, they have many local Pareto-optimal fronts, which makes it difficult to obtain a good divergence on the predicted values. It is important to note that the models had a greater divergence of values in the problems with 10 objectives, demonstrating a shape closer to the ideal. This is mainly due to the increased number of features used for training which makes the models perform better than with « objectives. The DTLZ6 problem, Figure 20, is the case that the predicted objectives are a little far away from the ideal. DTLZ6 has a degenerate Pareto-optimal front like DTLZ5, besides that, the DTLZ6 has many locals Pareto fronts which makes it difficult to converge to the Pareto-optimal front. Concerning the strategy of using 1 or /u1D45B models to estimate each decision variable, the results show that both strategies can be used. In different optimization problems, each one gets the best results.

The results found by the regression experiment are quite promising. Different models could learn the decision variables by a set of objective function values. Even in more restricted scenarios, the models achieved good results. For the scope of this work, the models and techniques used were enough to validate the learning of decision variables.

## 3.2.3 Optimization Experiment

In this experiment, we validate the DVL as an algorithm for Many-objective optimization. First, the same models are used to test the impact of different regression algorithms to optimize the DTLZ benchmark test suit. Then, the models that achieve goods results will be compared to the NSGA-III, a robust and well-known algorithm considered a state-of-the-art of MOEAs.

Each algorithm runs until it reaches a stop condition, in the experiments we use the number of evaluations of the objective function as a stop condition. A set of a maximum number of evaluations to our experiment is defined as (250, 500, 1000, 1500, and 10000), all algorithms run with the same number of calls to the objective function. For each maximum number of evaluations, the algorithms are executed 20 times independently to later perform the statistical comparison. This validation set is used to simulate different scenarios of restrictions in the use of the objective function. In this set, we classify as a higher restriction level a number of

The empirical comparisons between the results are made by the use of Hypervolume (HV) (WHILE et al., 2006), a performance indicator that assesses both convergence and divergence of the solutions. Let /u1D466 ∗ be a reference point dominated by all the Pareto front solutions, and /u1D443 the population resulting of a MOEA. The HV of /u1D443 is the calculus of the volume of the region that dominates /u1D466 ∗ and is dominated by /u1D443 . The HV values presented in this work are all normalized to [0, 1] by dividing ∏ /u1D45A /u1D456 = 1 /u1D466 ∗ /u1D456 . Table 12 shows the reference points set that are used for each DTLZ problem. Generally, the reference points have values close to zero, well below the values used in this experiment. But, due to the restriction that we imposed on the maximum number of evaluations, the reference point must have higher values. In the literature, for example, the optimization algorithms execute around 100000 to 1 million objective function evaluations. While in our experiment, the maximum number of evaluations is 10000.

The parameters used in NSGA-III were defined by the pymoo (Blank; Deb, 2020), which is a python framework for optimization. For the simulated binary crossover (DEB; AGRAWAL et al., 1995), the distribution index is set to /u1D702 /u1D450 = 30 , and the crossover probability /u1D45D /u1D450 = 1 . 0 . For the polynomial mutation (DEB; GOYAL, 1996), the distribution index and the mutation probability are set to /u1D702 /u1D45A = 20 and /u1D45D /u1D45A = 1 / /u1D45B , respectively, as recommended in (DEB, 2001). The population size used was 91 and 220 for the problem with « and 10 objectives, respectively, and the individual has a length of 12 for both objective sizes.

The results of the optimization experiment for « and 10 objectives are shown in Tables 1» and 15, respectively. Each line represents the values of the mean and standard deviation of the

20 executions of each algorithm per scenario of restriction. The best results are highlighted in bold if more than one value is highlighted, then it means that there is no statistically significant difference between these results. In comparison to the regression experiment, is possible to note that the models that have the best MSE not always achieved the best results of hypervolume. For « objectives, only the SVR and the MO-Linear models achieved good results of hypervolume in DTLZ1, DTLZ«, and DTLZ7, just as they obtained in the regression experiment. For 10 objectives, no model that got the best result in the regression experiment achieved the best HV mean. What draws the most attention is the performance of the SVR and the two MLP versions, MLP and MO-MLP, who achieved good results in « and 10 objectives. Mainly because although the MLP does not obtain the lowest MSE value, the generated solutions have a good diversity which implies a better HV. Besides that, the architecture of the DVL algorithm allows new training at each iteration with objectives closer to the ideal. As the model is reused during iterations, this task can be seen as transfer learning and many studies have demonstrated the superior performance of neural networks compared to statistical methods in transfer learning (LU et al., 2015).

These problems are characterized by having Pareto-optimal fronts with different shapes from the previous ones. The case of DTLZ5 and DTLZ6 both have degenerated Pareto-optimal fronts, and DTLZ7 has a disconnected front. These kinds of problems make it difficult for MOEAs to find the ideal frontier.

The results of the experiment with 10 objectives show that the DVL algorithm was superior in the vast majority of cases, except for the case of the DTLZ» problem with 10000 evaluations, in which the NSGA-III is superior to the DVL with any model. Table 16 summarizes the results of the statistical comparison in terms of wins, draws, and losses. A win means that the algorithm has the best-isolated result, no other is statistically comparable to it. A draw means that the algorithm has the best result and it is statistically comparable with others. And a loss means that the algorithm has not achieved the best value and it is not statistically comparable with the best result. The heat maps of the statistical comparison of this experiment can be seen in Appendix-Section A. It is possible to note the DVL superiority in problems with 10 objectives by winning «« of «5 scenarios. With the MLP model having 2« wins in comparison to the others. In the experimentation with « objectives, the NSGA-III wins a total of 1« in «5, and the combination of all DVL different models wins 15. This shows that the DVL can also be used for optimization in problems with a lower number of objectives. We can deduce from the experiments that the

DVL has a good performance in different kinds of problems with different Pareto-optimal shapes, search space sizes, with different local and global optimal, and a different number of decision variables. According to the experiments, this last characteristic, the number of decision variables, is a key factor for the greater performance of the DVL in comparison to the NSGA-III. The results also show that the strategy used for learning as well as the model is problem-dependent. In different scenarios, different strategies got better results, with the MO-MLP, and MLP having the best overall between these strategies.

The overall result found is quite promising, the DVL produced a valuable performance against the NSGA-III in many scenarios, even though the DVL algorithm is recent and also it needs greater maturity for optimization tasks. It is observed that different from the NSGA-III, the DVL does not behave like a search algorithm for optimization. The hypervolume of the solutions generated by the DVL is not always been improved by the increase of iterations. This means that there is a lack of local search to improve the solutions found near the Pareto-optimal front. Another point is that the reference points used by the DVL may not be close to the Pareto-optimal front which can lead to unwanted values of decision variables. Research on the algorithm architecture to improve the DVL can lead to even better results.

## 4 DVL Framework

In the previous chapter, it was demonstrated that the inverse model is experimentally capable of estimating the Pareto front in diverse optimization problems. So it is possible to proceed to the next step, in this chapter, we propose a DVL variation that can be used in integration with MOEAs, and design a framework that abstracts this integration. We believe that this approach can lead to the improvement of both algorithms, producing better results in solving optimization problems. The DVL algorithm can benefit from the MOEA due to its global search strategies and adaptation to the Pareto front of the problem. The MOEA can benefit from the DVL due to its high capacity for a global understanding of the problem, achieving a high convergence to the PF with a low number of evaluations, as we showed in Chapter «. We also compare the proposed DVL Framework integrated with some well-known MOEAs and apply it to solve several multi-objective optimization problems, from benchmark to real optimization problems. The goal is to validate the proposed framework and evaluate its ability to improve the performance of well-known algorithms in the literature.

To improve the algorithm limitations and leverage its strengths, we propose a DVL Framework that uses a DVL variation that can be executed in cooperation with an MOEA. The main reason to create a framework instead of an algorithm is due to the capacity to abstract the implementation, integrate with other algorithms, and provide a generic functionality, in this case, providing an initial set of solutions to any MOEA of the literature. Figure 22 presents the overall algorithm framework. The DVL Framework is based on two main steps, the first one is the use of DVL inverse modeling. The key idea is to use the good performance in restrictive scenarios of the DVL algorithm to estimate an initial set of solutions to the MOEA. The second step is the use of the initial set, which is an approximation of the Pareto-optimal provided by the DVL, to the MOEA to continue the optimization process until it reaches a pre-determined time or number of evaluations. In the end, a final population set, which represents the predicted set of the Pareto-optimal front, is outputted by the framework.

The first one has a higher abstraction level and provides the overall pseudocode of the framework. The second one references the new implementation of the DVL inverse modeling, which has been modified to work in the DVL Framework. The pseudocode of the framework is described in Algorithm 2.

## 4.2 Experiments and Results

In this section, we evaluate the new strategy of using the DVL as a framework for inverse modeling in combination with an MOEA. The motivation is to validate the DVL algorithm as a strategy for producing initial solutions as close as possible to the Pareto-optimal front. Due to its capacity of global understanding of the problem with a low number of evaluations. The performance of the DVL Framework is compared to the default implementation of the DVL algorithm, and also, with state-of-the-art MOEAs used in the literature. We use different MOEA approaches to deal with optimization problems, such as the NSGA-III as a candidate for Pareto-based approach, the MOEA/D as a decomposition-based algorithm, and the RVEA as a reference vector-guided algorithm. Also, these MOEAs are used inside the DVL Framework in our experiments. The DVL algorithm and the DVL Framework are tested in the Traffic Lights Signaling optimization problem described in Section ».2.1.1. Different from the previous experiments, this real optimization problem has an expensive objective function and constraints which provides a new scenario of study the DVL inverse modeling.

## 4.2.1 Optimization Problems

Two different kinds of optimization problems are used in the experiments of the DVL Framework. The first set of problems is the first seven test problems from the DTLZ benchmark testȷ DTLZ1 to DTLZ7, already described in our previous experiments in Section «.2. We also maintain the configuration of the DTLZ instances for this experiment, one with « objectives and 12 variables and the other with 10 objectives and 12 variables. This kind of optimization problem gives us support in the initial analysis of the DVL Framework.

The second type of optimization problem used in the DVL Framework experiment is the problem of traffic light signaling modeled as an MaOP, a real-world expensive many-objective optimization problem. This problem is characterized by having many objectives, a costly objective function, constraints, and an unknown Pareto-optimal set. This problem is well described below to improve the understanding for later use in our experiments. The use of an experiment of this kind is important to analyze the performance of the DVL Framework and also the DVL in a scenario never tested before.

## 4.2.1.1 Traffic Lights Signaling: A Many-Objective Optimization Problem

The Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) aim to improve transportation through the use of technologies. One of its areas of improvement is traffic management, where the efficiency can be improved by using data from the roads and the traffic to optimize the efficiency, safety, and quality of the traffic flow, for example, by reducing traffic congestion and travel time. Traffic light signaling optimization is one way of improving traffic efficiency. It relies on optimizing the traffic-light cycle, which is the sequence of states that a traffic light has (SĂNCHEZ-

MEDINA; GALĂN-MORENO; RUBIO-ROYO, 2009). To obtain the data of the traffic flow a traffic simulator can be used. A well-known traffic simulator is SUMO (Simulation of Urban Mobility) (KRAJZEWICZ; BONERT; WAGNER, 2006) which provides all the data necessary to simulate a traffic flow, manage the traffic-light cycle, and obtain several traffic quality measures such as travel and stopped time, the number of vehicles that arrive at their destination, the overall average speed, and traffic flow, carbon dioxide emission, among others.

In traffic lights signaling the synchronization is achieved when two or more traffic lights are running in a manner that allows a vehicle to pass the traffic lights synchronized without stops. Traffic light signal optimization in general is a very complex problem, even for a single intersection can be no obvious optimal solution. The synchronization will not always ensure that vehicles will pass through open traffic lights. In this problem, it is possible to use several traffic quality measures as objective functions. But, the majority of the related work only selects a small set of objective functions (often two). This limitation on the number of objective functions lies in the incapacity of traditional MOEA to deal with a high number of objective functions. In this work, we modeled this problem as a MaOP with 6 objective functions to approximate the modeling of real situations through the use of simulators, since it is important to consider different quality measures when defining traffic-light cycles.

In the representation of the problem of traffic light synchronization modeled as a MaOP, it is necessary to give a combination of traffic lights to build a computational representation of the duration of each phase for each traffic light. The duration may assume a finite interval, usually with few options, e.g, in our study, it assumes a range from four to one hundred and twenty. The decision variables are the time of each phase of each traffic light, and the objective functions are the traffic-related quality measures calculated by the simulator. The computational representation of the duration time of the traffic light phases can assume a mathematical representation using a solution vector, x , of integer variables, such thatȷ x = ( /u1D436 1 1 , /u1D436 1 2 , ..., /u1D436 1 /u1D45B , /u1D436 2 1 , ..., /u1D436 2 /u1D45B , /u1D436 /u1D45A 1 , ..., /u1D436 /u1D45A /u1D45B ) , where /u1D436 /u1D458 /u1D457 represents the duration, /u1D451 , of the /u1D457 /u1D461ℎ phase (optimizable) of the /u1D458 /u1D461ℎ intersection and 20 ≤ /u1D451 ≤ 100 , /u1D451 ∈ N . From each solution x , the simulator calculates the values of the m-objective functions to form the objective vector /u1D453 ( x ) = ( /u1D453 1 ( x ) , /u1D453 2 ( x ) , ..., /u1D453 /u1D45A ( x )) which will be later evaluated by the search algorithm.

Thus, it is possible to treat the traffic light synchronization problem as an optimization problem, representing a computationally possible combination of the phase times of the traffic lights through a vector. Figure 2« shows all elements of the vector. These elements must be within the range contained in the lower ( /u1D459 ) and upper ( /u1D462 ) limits of the 'green phases' duration. For each intersection (ranging from 1 to /u1D45A ), the size of the vector to be optimized will be formed by the phases (ranging from 1 to /u1D45B ) where, in at least one direction, one has a green state, a 'green phase'. This implies that the phase in which the directions are formed only by red states, or only by yellow and red states, will have its time set to » seconds and will not be used in the vector.

## 4.2.2 Algorithms, Parameters and quality metrics

In this experiment, the same procedures of the optimization experiment in Section «.2.« are followed. Each algorithm runs until reaches a maximum number of evaluations, defined as (250, 500, 1000, 1500, 10000, 100000). Different from the previous experiment, the value of 100000 maximum number of evaluations was added to validate the DVL and the DVL Framework in scenarios where the MOEAs have good results. The empirical comparisons between the results are made by the use of Hypervolume (HV) (WHILE et al., 2006), a performance indicator that assesses both convergence and divergence of the solutions. Different from the previous experiment, a new reference points set is used with values closer to the Optimal-front. Table 17 shows the reference points set used in this experiment for each DTLZ problem. The motivation to use this new set is to achieve more precision and detail in the comparison of the results.

The parameters used and the implementations of the NSGA-III and MOEA/D algorithms were defined by the pymoo (Blank; Deb, 2020). For the NSGA-III, using simulated binary crossover (DEB; AGRAWAL et al., 1995), the distribution index is set to /u1D702 /u1D450 = 30 , and the crossover probability /u1D45D /u1D450 = 1 . 0 . For the polynomial mutation (DEB; GOYAL, 1996), the distribution index and the mutation probability are set to /u1D702 /u1D45A = 20 and /u1D45D /u1D45A = 1 / /u1D45B , respectively, as recommended in (DEB, 2001). For the MOEA/D algorithm, the number of the weight vectors in the neighborhood /u1D45B = 15 and the mating probability of two solutions in the neighborhood is set

to /u1D447 = 0 . 7 . For the RVEA algorithm, was used the python library pyRVEA (SAINI, 2019), which is a python implementation of the original version of the RVEA based in Cheng et al. (2016). The parameters used were, for the simulated binary crossover, the same as the NSGA-III algorithm, the distribution index is set to /u1D702 /u1D450 = 30 , and the crossover probability /u1D45D /u1D450 = 1 . 0 . And also the same as the NSGA-III for the polynomial mutation, the distribution index, and the mutation probability are set to /u1D702 /u1D45A = 20 and /u1D45D /u1D45A = 1 / /u1D45B , respectively. For all the algorithms the population size used was 91 and 220 for the problem with « and 10 objectives, respectively, and the individual has a length of 12 for both objective sizes.

## 4.2.3 Results and discussion

In this subsection, we analyze the results of the DVL Framework experiment on the DTLZ benchmark test suit. All the algorithms were executed 20 times independently for each restriction configuration in the number of evaluations. One of the parameters of the DVL Framework is the MOEA /u1D45A used in the optimization process after the DVL inverse modeling, in the experiments we use the same MOEAs running isolated and with the DVL Frameworkȷ NSGA-III, MOEA/D, and RVEA. With this, in addition to analyzing the performance of the framework competing with these algorithms, it is also possible to analyze the impact that the framework has on each one. In the results, the nomenclature DVL+NSGA-III represents the framework running with the NSGA-III as a parameter, while the nomenclature NSGA-III means the algorithm running by the default implementation.

The result of the DVL Framework experiment is separated into two parts. First, we analyze only the impact of the framework over the three MOEAsȷ NSGA-III, MOEA/D, and RVEA. Figures 2» and 25 show the percentage of the difference in the mean of hypervolume between the result of the MOEA integrated into the DVL Framework and the result of the MOEA in standalone. The blue bar for example, in each plot, demonstrates the percentage in hypervolume mean of the DVL Framework using the NSGA-III decreased by the value of the hypervolume mean of the NSGA-III. A positive value means that the DVL Framework improves the MOEA and a negative value means that the MOEA has a better result. The x-axis represents the maximum number of evaluations, and the y-axis is the percentage of improvement in the hypervolume mean over 20 runs of the algorithm.

Analyzing the impact of the DVL Framework on the algorithms is possible to note that the framework improves substantially the NSGA-III algorithm in the DTLZ1 and DTLZ« for both « and 10 objectives. These problems are characterized by having a high search space. And also, a substantial improvement in the DTLZ6 with « objectives, a degenerated problem. For the other degenerated problem, DTLZ5, the framework had a low impact. In all the other cases of the NSGA-III, the framework provided a good improvement, which comes close to zero improvement in the scenario of 100000 function evaluations. In some cases of this scenario, the algorithm standalone wins the framework, but the values are very close to each other. The results show that

the DVL Framework with the NSGA-III can be used instead of the NSGA-III standalone with a great improvement in performance. The MOEA/D is improved substantially in the DTLZ1 and DTLZ« for « and 10 objectives. The DTLZ» with 10 objectives is an interesting example that the MOEA/D had more improvements than the other algorithms. But in comparison to the others, in the rest of the problems, the MOEA/D has the lower values in impact. The MOEA/D has some examples where the DVL Framework has a loss in hypervolume, mainly the case of the DTLZ« with 10 objectives, and some cases of the DTLZ2 and DTLZ5 with « objectives, where is better to use the MOEA/D in standalone. But, in the scenarios where the DVL Framework loses, the values are very close to the MOEA, showing the good performance of the DVL Framework over the MOEA/D.

From the algorithms tested, the RVEA is the one that most benefits from the framework. In scenarios where the other algorithms have lower improvements, like DTLZ7 with « and 10 objectives, the framework had a great impact on the RVEA. The RVEA is the unique algorithm that obtains gains in the scenario of 100000 function evaluations, in the DTLZ6 and DTLZ7 with « objectives, and DTLZ2, DTLZ6, and DTLZ7 with 10 objectives. These are examples of problems with different shapes and search spaces. For the others cases of the RVEA, the framework provided a good improvement. Our hypothesis of the high impact of the DVL Framework in the RVEA is mainly due to the approximation of the estimated solution set provided by the DVL inverse model and the reference vectors used by the RVEA. The method that generates the reference points for the prediction of new solutions in the DVL inverse model is similar to the method that produces the reference vectors of the RVEA. With the initial solution set already closed to the reference vectors, the RVEA can better improve the search in terms of divergence and convergence. Another algorithm that uses the same method that generates reference points is the NSGA-III, but in this case, the algorithm uses the reference points only to ensure diversity in the obtained solutions. Because of this, the impact of the framework over the NSGA-III may have been smaller than on RVEA.

The results show that the DVL Framework has a positive impact on the MOEAs, in the vast majority of cases, the DVL Framework outperformed the MOEAs especially in the initial evaluations, approaching zero in the difference of hypervolume when it reaches 100000 objective function evaluations. The few exceptions that an MOEA surpassed the DVL Framework are the ones with the MOEA/D, these results are in some cases of the DTLZ2 and DTLZ5 with « objectives and DTLZ« with 10 objectives. This leads to greater security in the use of the framework, regardless of the scenario, the impact on the gain in hypervolume is greater than the loss. Making the framework a good choice to use instead of the MOEA standalone.

The second part of the analysis consists of the statistical comparison for « and 10 objectives shown in Tables 19 and 20, respectively. The heat maps of the statistical comparison of this experiment can be seen in Appendix-Section B. This experiment leads to an understanding in which situations the DVL, the DVL Framework, or the MOEA can be used. Analyzing the

result in different problems. For example, the DVL Framework with RVEA got the best results for the DTLZ1 problem with « and 10 objectives. The DVL Framework with NSGA-III has high hypervolume values in DTLZ2, DTLZ», DTLZ5, and DTLZ6 with « and 10 objectives, and

also in DTLZ7 with 10 objectives. For « objectives the DVL algorithm outstands in the DTLZ7 problem, performing better than the others in this kind of problem. In DTLZ2, DTLZ5, and DTLZ6 it is comparable to the DVL Framework with NSGA-III in most cases where there is a higher restriction in the number of validations of the objective function. For 10 objectives the DVL algorithm has good results in the DTLZ5 and DTLZ6 problems, being comparable to the DVL Framework with NSGA-III. The DVL Framework with MOEA/D obtains the best results in the DTLZ» and DTLZ6 for 10 objectives. Some differences in the DVL algorithm can be seen in this experiment in comparison with the previous, mainly due to the reference point set used. In this experiment, the reference set is more close to the ideal, leading to greater distances in the values of the results found. There are few cases where an MOEA wins over the DVL or the DVL Framework. For « objectives these cases are in the restriction scenario of 100000 evaluations, and for 10 objectives are mainly in the DTLZ« problem where the MOEA/D wins in different scenarios. This shows that the MOEA/D has a high performance in this kind of problem, converging fast to a value next to the reference point adopted.

## 4.2.4 Traffic Lights Signaling Experiment

The preview experiments demonstrate that both the DVL and the DVL Framework have good performance in a wide set of benchmark problems. But, during our analysis of these experiments, some research questions aroseȷ

1. What is the cost of training a machine learning model during a real expensive optimization problem?

## 2. How the algorithm will perform in face of an unknown Pareto-optimal front?

The use of the DTLZ benchmark test suite helps in the agility to produce experiments due to the easy usability of the suite. But these objective functions run in an insignificant processing time in comparison to the total time of running the algorithm which can cause differences in the results even when we use the maximum number of validations to compare the algorithms. In this section, we propose to compare the DVL algorithm, the DVL Framework, and an MOEA in a real expensive many-objective optimization problem, the Traffic Lights Signaling. The stop condition used in this experiment will be the total processing time of the algorithms. It will allow us to identify if there is a cost in training the models during the optimization, and also validate the DVL inverse model in a different scenario, where the Pareto-optimal front is unknown.

In the optimization problem of traffic light synchronization, the decision variables are the time of each phase of each traffic light and the objective functions are the traffic-related quality measures calculated by the simulator. The scenario used in this experiment is represented by Figure 26, based on the experiments proposed by Matos &amp; Carvalho ( 2016). Each intersection is configured with a two-phase traffic light. The phases schema and number of roads are the same at all intersections. Each intersection is crossed with 2 two-way roads, where each road has 6 lanes, i.e. « lanes for each way (direction). The solution is represented by an eight-position integer vector (n = 8), since each of the four intersections has two 'green' phases, totalizing 2 decision variables for each intersection. Each value represents the duration of the phase assuming a finite interval in the range from twenty to one hundred and twenty. For the simulation, 21000 vehicles were used. The vehicles are inserted into the simulation through the injectors, located at the extremities, numbered by 1 to 8 in Figure 26. The distribution of the vehicle flows in the injectors was defined at random before initiating any simulation and thus maintained in all experiments. If the distribution between the injectors were not maintained for the different experiments, the results would be different in the end. The total time to be simulated, for each execution, was 1 hour, but in the SUMO simulator, it is possible to speed up this time to approximately 10 seconds of clock time or 0.2« of processing time. This time represents one execution of the objective function evaluation. At the end the simulator outputs the six objective functionsȷ

- Depart delay ȷ The time the vehicle had to wait before it could start his journey;
- Trip duration ȷ The time the vehicle needed to accomplish the route;
- Wait steps ȷ The number of steps in which the vehicle speed was below 0.1m/s;
- Time loss ȷ The time lost due to driving below the ideal speed (60km/h);
- CO abs ȷ complete amount of /u1D436 /u1D442 (in milligram) emitted by the vehicle during the trip;
- /u1D436 /u1D442 2 abs ȷ The complete amount of /u1D436 /u1D442 2 emitted by the vehicle during the trip;

Figure 26 - Traffic light synchronization scenario.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Sourceȷ Produced by authors.

In this experiment three algorithms will be testedȷ the NSGA-II algorithm (DEB et al., 2002a), which has good results in this kind of problem in comparison to the NSGA-III algorithm (MATOS; CARVALHO, 2016), the DVL algorithm, and the DVL Framework with the NSGA-II algorithm. The algorithms are executed independently 20 times for each configuration an theFriedman's test followed by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test is adopted to compare the results between each configuration of the experiments with a value of 0.05 of the significance level. The best results in the following table will be highlighted in bold, if more than one value is highlighted in bold it means that there is no statistically significant difference between the result and the best value. Each algorithm runs until it reaches a stop condition, different from the previous experiments, in this experiment we use the processing time as a stop condition. This time represents the sum of the system and user CPU time of the current process. A set of a maximum number of processing time is defined as (70, 220, and 1100) in fractional seconds. This validation set is used to simulate different scenarios of restrictions in the use of the processing time. The empirical comparisons between the results are made by the use of Hypervolume, which is calculated by considering a nadir point as the reference point. In this experiment, the nadir was obtained considering all values obtained in all executions. The overall execution of this experiment took a total of approximately »» days to complete.

The DVL algorithm and the DVL Framework were modified to attend to this experiment. A parameter /u1D460 were added that represents a stop condition, the maximum process time that the algorithm can run, this parameter has different values for each configuration of the experiment.

For the other parameters, the DVL algorithm is configured as the /u1D450 value is fixed in 200, the /u1D716 is set to 0.001, and the /u1D458 value is set to 250. For the DVL Framework the value of the parameter /u1D458 is 250, and the MOEA /u1D45A used is the NSGA-II. The implementation and the parameters used in the NSGA-II were defined by the pymoo (Blank; Deb, 2020). For the simulated binary crossover, the distribution index is set to /u1D702 /u1D450 = 15 , and the crossover probability /u1D45D /u1D450 = 0 . 9 . For the polynomial mutation, the distribution index and the mutation probability are set to /u1D702 /u1D45A = 20 and /u1D45D /u1D45A = 1 / /u1D45B , respectively.

In Table 21 is demonstrated the difference in number of evaluations of each algorithm per configuration of the experiment. It can be seen that the DVL algorithm and the DVL Framework have a lower number of evaluations in comparison to the NSGA-II. In more restrictive scenarios this difference is smaller but increases in less restrictive scenarios, with the increase of the processing time. This difference in the number of calls of the function evaluation is mainly due to the time spent the DVL has to train the models and predicting new solutions. Table 22 presents the results of the Traffic Lights Signaling Experiment by showing the mean and the standard deviation of the hypervolume obtained during the 20 runs. The result of this experiment demonstrates a similarity with the previous experiments, where the DVL algorithm shows good performance in more restrictive scenarios while the DVL Framework has a better overall performance, even with a smaller number of objective function calls.

Also, the results found indicates a greater safety and reliability of the results obtained in the previous experiments that used the DTLZ benchmark test suit. In the restriction scenario of 70 processing time, the DVL algorithm and the DVL Framework have the better result and both are statistically comparable. For 220 and 1100, the DVL Framework has the best results. It is possible to note the efficiency of the DVL inverse model in finding good solutions as close as possible to the optimal values even in a restricted scenario. The difference between the hypervolume mean in the 70 process time and 1100 is not so far, but the DVL Framework has good results by using the efficiency of the MOEA in finding good local optima improving the overall hypervolume. The statistical comparison that results in this experiment can be seen in Figure 27.
