## 5

## Conclusion

Machine Learning enhancing metaheuristic algorithms is an open topic of the literature that can produce knowledge and open research topic in the major areas of Machine Learning and Optimization. In this work, we explore this area in a systematic review that presents relevant results to guide future research in the field. We show that the number of publications has increased over the last ten years, the majority in journals, which shows the maturity of the research area. Most approaches are focused on decreasing the number of objective function validations during the search. And the most used type of algorithms is the SAEAs and EDAs.

Within this area, our topic of research was specifically the inverse models, an approach that uses an inverse functional mapping from the Pareto Front to the Pareto Set. The DVL algorithm was our main topic of work, it is an approach of inverse modeling designed to generate solutions as close as possible to the Pareto-optimal front. Due to the study of the DVL being recent and the necessity of proving the algorithm, we conduct a set of experiments, based on previously established hypotheses, to validate the algorithm and find its strengths and weaknesses. So in this work, we showed experimentally that the DVL algorithm and its strategy of inverse modeling can compete with well-known MOEAs of the literature, such as the NSGA-III in the optimization of benchmark problems. Experimental results demonstrate that the inverse model can estimate the Pareto-optimal front of the DTLZ benchmark test suit problems, and also, the DVL algorithm can outperform the NSGA-III algorithm in restrictive scenarios, i.e. with restrictions on the number of evaluations, and problems with a higher number of objectives.

Due to the good performance of the DVL algorithm in restrictive scenarios, we propose a DVL Framework that uses a DVL variation that can be executed with an MOEA. The key idea of the framework is to use the DVL to estimate an initial solution set as close as possible to the Pareto-optimal set. After this step, the MOEA continues the search to find better local optima. With the implementation of the DVL Framework in hand, we evaluate it in the optimization experimentation. Where different combinations of the framework are compared to the DVL

algorithm and different MOEAs of the literature. The results show that the DVL Framework can improve the MOEAs in a wide range of scenarios, according to our experiments, up to a limit of 100000 objective function evaluations. The choice of which MOEA uses in the DVL Framework is dependent on the problem. Also, our results shows that the DVL algorithm can be used in some scenarios of higher restriction in the number of validations and in problems that have degenerated or disconnected Pareto-optimal fronts.

Finally, we evaluate the two algorithms in a real-world optimization expensive problem. A problem of this kind can show different results from the previous experiments mainly due to its constraints in the problem, the expensive time to evaluate the objective function, and the unknown Pareto-optimal front which can have a shape different from the previous problems. The experiment is conducted on the optimization problem of traffic light synchronization. The algorithms are compared with the NSGA-II algorithm, which has good results in this problem with the same scenario used. The results show that, even if the DVL inverse model spent time in training and predicting solutions, this time lost is minimal compared to the hypervolume gain with the solutions set proposed by the algorithm. In a more restrictive scenario, with a processing time of 70, the DVL algorithm and the DVL Framework have the best result, and in the other scenarios, the DVL Framework outperformed the other algorithms.

The results found in this work demonstrate a promising area of research in inverse modeling. The DVL algorithm and the DVL Framework show good results in diverse scenarios of different problems. For future works, we suggest the improvement of the weak points of the DVL algorithm, such as the deterioration of the search performance, other forms of improving the iterative process of the DVL algorithm can be analyzed to improve the local optima. Also, the investigation of better shapes of the reference points or using a dynamic reference point set. Different problems have different formats of the Pareto-optimal front, the shape of the reference point can greatly influence the result obtained from the DVL. For the DVL Framework, we suggest a wide comparison with other MOEAs, and a full investigation of the restriction point that the inverse model has no more improvements over the MOEA.

We also believe that exploring the DVL inverse modeling in a different manner could lead to future works. The DVL Framework proposed in this work uses the inverse model in the Population Initialization component, as detailed in Chapter 2. But the DVL inverse model could also be used for Population Reproduction and Variation, where the inverse model could extract knowledge to improve the generation of new solutions. And in the Local Search, which could explore the inverse modeling to improve local populations. Future works can also explore, in a deeper way, models with more robust techniques of machine learning such as ensemble learning, deep learning, and others.
